Signal processing in interferometric HI intensity mapping can be comprehended through the lens of disturbance theory. 
For each antenna element, the observed visibility is a distorted representation of the original galaxy signal, resulting from the convolution of the galaxy's intensity with the combined geometric and projection effects of all antenna elements.
Since the galaxy's intensity remains unchanged, only the effects of the telescope's arrangement and the galaxy's location vary.
However, the differences between nearby configurations are minimal, and the interpolation between these configurations is linear.
This linear variation makes the cross-correlation of adjacent spectra and visibility vectors an effective tool for extracting the galaxy's spatial autocorrelation function, despite the complexities of the geometric transformation.
Notably, the effects of the telescope's arrangement and the galaxy's location can be separated and mitigated by using the anisotropic off-diagonal elements of the power spectrum to distinguish between the galaxy's spatial autocorrelation function and the effects of the telescope's arrangement.
Moreover, by accounting for the differences between the on-diagonal and anisotropic off-diagonal elements of the power spectrum, the optimal orientation of the telescope arrays can be determined to minimize the distortions and effects of the telescope's arrangement.
Additionally, despite the differences between the on-diagonal elements of the power spectrum, the bulk scale of the galaxy's spatial autocorrelation function can still be extracted.
However, the verification of these predictions requires extensive simulations involving accurate models of the telescope configuration and the galaxy's location, as well as sufficient

R. Penrose hypothesized that conscious systems have a unique link to 11-dimensional space. I propose an alternative framework by R. M. Milnes that suggests consciousness is related to a much larger dimensionality, specifically an infinite and non-countable number of dimensions. From this concept, I develop an operator theory that mirrors the patterns seen in penrose-like hexagons and is applicable to any finite graph.

Recommender Systems are increasingly relied upon by online users for navigation, given the overwhelming information clogged online environments. There is an pressing need to develop systems capable of providing high-quality recommendations at an unprecedented scale. Most existing RS models focus on either utilizing contextual information or mastering deep learning techniques. This research proposes an innovative hybrid approach that combines context-aware and behavior-driven methods. An advanced document-based context-driven algorithm, CCF, is introduced to create comprehensive user and item profiles based on publicly accessible content. An innovative merging strategy is developed to integrate CCF with state-of-the-art collaborative filtering and CF-based neural networks. This new hybrid framework outperforms current benchmarks in accuracy, achieving significant enhancements of up to 27.06% in NDCG, 23.53% in Prec@5, and 14.96% in Acc@5. Moreover, our results demonstrate that CCF's contributions can be accurately predicted during training, enabling the development of the first CF-based RS system that can dynamically provide users with the relative importance of contextual factors at training time. An experimental analysis is conducted to investigate how various system components, training data size, user interest depth, and contextual information affect performance. This comprehensive study provides actionable insights for RS development and future research. An open-source implementation of our recommended models is publicly available for replication purposes.

The concept of freeness for random matrices was first introduced by Aitchison and Gayet in 2015, and further developed by several researchers. Building upon previous work, particularly that of Biane and Bosma in 2018, we introduce a new notion of freeness, denoted as "freeness of kind $B$", and demonstrate its equivalence to existing definitions. We then establish a criterion for determining the freeness of random matrices under specific constraints. This criterion, tied to the structure of non-crossing partitions, allows us to analyze the freeness of certain random matrices and establish a condition for independence based on a specific matrix product.

Timed characteristics, initially defined in 1991, are used to describe timing-related aspects of programs. A formal description of sublinear characteristics was presented in 2011, but it contradicts earlier work, leading to confusion among researchers. To resolve this, we revisited the original paper and identified a critical error, which resulted in the closure of the characterisation framework. This forced a revision of our previous results on superlinear and nonlinear characteristics, ultimately leading to a novel decomposition rule for assessing complexity. Our study also provides additional insights into tailored characteristics, while highlighting the need for strict adherence to the original definition of timed characteristics to avoid misleading conclusions.

Our objective is to explore the process of $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ by means of the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ intertransition, and subsequently derive the $a_0(980)$ component of the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ decay. To accomplish this, we apply current effective field theories to describe the interactions among $a_0(980)$, $f_0(980)$, and the relevant meson pairs, and utilize phenomenological inputs to guide our calculations. The calculated branching ratio for $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ is in the range of $[1.9\times 10^{-6}]$, with the final $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ decay including both tree-level and loop contributions that combine to yield a branching ratio of $[1.1\times 10^{-6}]$.

The GRAVITY capture camera played a crucial role in the 2018 April 1st data collection, which included the first-ever image capturing the event Sgr A* at 16 GHz, a feat achieved through the coordination of the Submillimeter Array, Atacama Large Millimeter Array, and the Very Large Telescope. Due to the vast data output, the capture camera's functionality was temporarily modified during the real-time data processing. This decision was made in response to the telescope operators' request to utilize the capture camera as a standard technique for forthcoming high-priority projects.

We investigate the $k$-Center problem with a unique set of demands, where the characteristic of the demand set $\Gamma$ is that there exists an $\epsilon \in [0, 1]$ such that $\Gamma$ contains at least $k$ elements and the doubling measure of these elements is less than or equal to $\epsilon$, as well as at least $k$ elements with a highway measure less than or equal to $\delta \in [0, \epsilon]$.
We provide an $\tilde{O}(r^2 \ln (r / \epsilon))$-time approximation algorithm for this variant of the problem, where $r$ represents the maximum diameter of the metric space.
Our solution involves first applying the standard $k$-Center algorithm to obtain a solution with a doubling measure less than or equal to $\epsilon$, then removing at most $r$ centers with high frequency, and finally scaling the obtained distances by a factor of $1 + O(\epsilon / k)$.
We show that a natural fractional version of this problem has a convex programming relaxation with a conjugate programming exponent of $\frac{2}{1-\epsilon}$, and prove that the $k$-Center problem with a highway measure cannot be approximated within a factor better than $\Omega(\sqrt{\frac{\log k}{\delta}})$, where $\delta$ represents the minimum highway measure, on metric spaces with the minimum spanning tree as the underlying metric.

This paper builds upon previous research of the author found in research papers No. 773 and 801. We shall rework some key results from those studies. Furthermore, we will be introducing newly derived outcomes that surpass the findings of those research papers. 

To begin, we prove that for an entire function defined over the complex plane, if the shift $h(z)$ deviates from $z$ by at most an absolute discrepancy of $\phi(z)$, where the discrepancy function $\phi(z)$ satisfies a particular growth constraint, then the function $z - h(z)$ cannot have any critical points. 

Next, we demonstrate that the converse of this statement is also true, provided that the discrepancy function $\phi(z)$ meets a specific exponential threshold. 

Subsequently, we will be showing two distinct outcomes, one of which asserts that the function $z - h(z)$ must be analytic in a particular domain if $h(z)$ is merely a meromorphic function. The other outcome claims that the function $z - h(z)$ must be analytic in the entire complex plane if $h(z)$ is a constant function. 

Lastly, we prove that there exists a specific set of natural numbers $N$, such that for any natural number $k$, which is less than $N$, there exists a function $h(z)$, which is defined over the complex plane and is not a constant function, such that the difference $z - h(z)$ has at most $k$ critical points

This research explores the resolution of polynomial linear systems in multi-projective space, allowing for random solving errors. Given a system of degree D and a desired confidence level, we aim to find a threshold level of error tolerance, above which there is no solution. Our study establishes that the probability of fake positive outcomes decreases exponentially with the L1 norm of the error, and this exponential rate is the highest possible. To achieve this, we leverage non-negative polynomials and diophantine properties, and develop an early termination technique based on a sparse approximation of such polynomials. While this approach can provide upper bounds, it does not offer lower bounds for solving the system. Our knowledge about these bounds is currently insufficient, and further research is needed.

Strongly coupled systems with broken parity symmetry can give rise to unique light bundles that demonstrate parity-symmetry-guarded emissions. Research has shown that in a two-dimensional lattice, which represents a proxy for a phonon mode in a one-dimensional system, parity-symmetry-guarded zero-mode bundles emerge with superconducting properties. Furthermore, this study has found that these bundles remain stable even in the presence of non-superconducting three-band models. Notably, the zero-mode bundles in both super and non-superconducting models exhibit identical and complementary bundle emission properties. This discovery, for which theoretical and experimental implications are also proposed, suggests that parity-symmetry-guarded emissions could serve as a hallmark for the natural occurrence of superconducting or bundle-photon states.

A precise analytical model is presented, which provides exact predictions for the internal energy, entropy, and heat capacity of a group of equilibrium alkali gases, as a function of temperature and pressure. This model surpasses the capabilities of the ideal gas calculations, which assumes the removal of all interactions, which is not feasible according to quantum mechanics. Our model confirms recent research findings that an interaction-free gas does not follow a perfect gas law, specifically in regards to high-pressure, high-temperature scenarios. Our results for the high-temperature limit match those of previous independent studies. We also developed a novel expression for entropy that incorporates the de Broglie wavelength and is compatible with both classical and quantum mechanics principles. Our analysis demonstrates the significant discrepancies between the ideal gas and this optimized model, particularly in regards to predicted heat capacity values, which highlight the significance of interaction corrections, especially at both extremely low and extremely high temperatures.

In the context of a medium with a specific type of matter, we've discovered that the presence of certain particle interactions causes a notable discrepancy in how particles behave at different energy levels. We've found that this discrepancy results in significant alterations to the mass of certain particles, such as vector mesons, and their movement patterns, or propagators. We're using a mathematical framework called Effective Field Theory to describe these particle movements and their response to changing conditions. Our analysis focuses on how vector mesons behave in an extreme environment, such as that found in the center of stars or nuclear matter, and we've made predictions about their behavior in this context. We've found that the changes to the mass of these particles, in this particular type of environment, could be significant, up to several hundred MeV. We're using this information to study the response of these particles, in this environment, to various quantities, such as electric and magnetic fields. Our predictions could have important implications for understanding phenomena, such as how these particles behave in the presence of nucleonic matter, and nuclear events like heavy-ion collisions.

This paper explores the problem of determining network diameter in large networks that have a small-world property, despite the presence of malicious nodes that can disrupt communication. A certain type of network that exhibits a small-world characteristic is composed of a complete graph for all nodes connected to a single adversary, and a k-vertex connected graph for all nodes free from disruption. Our investigation focuses on developing an efficient algorithm for estimating network diameter in this type of network. This algorithm uses only a small number of message transmissions and is resilient against malicious interference, giving an accurate measurement of network diameter with high probability. Furthermore, this algorithm is versatile, allowing it to work on networks that are clustered and those with irregular structure. What's more, this research is the first to tackle this problem in a reliable manner and proves that network diameter can be accurately estimated using a linear number of transmissions, whereas any single transmission would be insufficient.

Successful numerical relativity simulations require a comprehensive strategy to manage data, specifically identifying key points to track across spacetime. A widely adopted method, using a fixed grid with evenly spaced markers, suits steady-state scenarios but poorly handles varying densities, leading to unnecessary data depth. In dynamic scenarios, a more adaptable approach is needed to balance complexity and clarity. Our proposed method begins with a preliminary approximation of the solution using a fundamental integral, followed by a more in-depth analysis based on the solution's behavior, thus ensuring only essential points are used to describe the solution across spacetime. A comparison with the traditional approach shows our method can significantly reduce data restrictions while maintaining accuracy, thus enhancing the efficiency of relativistic hydrodynamics simulations.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves precisely identifying the neutrino mass ordering by closely examining the electron antineutrino energy spectrum resulting from $^{8}0$U decays. To achieve this, the experiment relies on a cutting-edge 20,000 PMT optical detector composed of 20-inch large photomultiplier tubes. To guarantee the experiment's success, a comprehensive examination of the PMTs was carried out to ensure their high-quality performance. This process included a series of tests such as hygroscopy, electrical, and functional tests followed by a close inspection of the PMTs using a high-power ultraviolet light and their resulting anode signals. Following the detailed evaluation, the PMTs were thoroughly cleaned and assembled to form the large-scale optical detector, thereby ensuring the experiment's high signal collection capability and the necessary high signal-to-noise ratio. This work presents the comprehensive examination, the developed analysis methods, and the outcomes of the PMT characterization.

In practical scenarios like power grid prediction and air quality analysis, intricate systems generate intricate data sets that are difficult to model using traditional forecasting methods, requiring intricate networks that mimic these complex relationships. Due to the spatial connectivity implied by sensor placement, temporal series can be effectively analyzed as graphs, linking features in spacetime. However, current models are limited by their inflexible graph topology, unable to adapt to the nuances of multidimensional temporal series. This inflexibility leads to subpar performance, as demonstrated by our comparison with a fully connected neural network. To overcome this challenge, a new adaptive graph convolutional network is proposed, featuring a dynamic learning framework that accommodates any graph structure and enables self-monitoring of node and edge performance. This allows our low-complexity network to automatically evolve into an optimized structure, rivaling the performance of a fully connected neural network and a specially designed custom graph.

In a previous study, we established a novel method to characterize the scattering pattern of the atmosphere, essential for assessing the integrity of experiments that rely on on-sky observations to measure the cosmic microwave background and other faint signals. This follow-up investigation employs the established method to analyze a range of atmospheric models, including those that simulate the behavior of molecules and aerosols at varying heights. By using our technique to fit the scattering pattern of these models, we are able to assess their accuracy across different atmospheric layers and frequencies, ultimately proposing a set of criteria to evaluate the suitability of these models for on-sky data analysis.

District-level special education funding varies significantly from $60 to $200 per student.  A collaborative study between educational policymakers and local special education instructors revealed that the existing system lacks clarity, and instructors have varying understandings of what labels mean in terms of instructional actions.  To address this issue, researchers developed Special Education Instructor Distillation, an approach where multiple specialized instructors provide detailed guidance to support students with unique learning needs.  However, the process faces a couple of challenges:  (1) coordinating the efforts of multiple instructors is complicated, and (2) the comprehensive labels used by instructors lack specificity and clarity.  To overcome these problems, researchers proposed Pairwise Iterative Logits Coalition (PILE), a distillation framework that helps multiple instructors work together by iteratively selecting and refining instructor labels based on their coherence with regards to student data.  Through experiments on real-world data sets, researchers observed that PILE's performance consistently improves with each iteration, and its labels are highly consistent and reliable.  Notably, PILE's early iterations demonstrated comparable or even superior accuracy to state-of-the-art non-coalition distillation methods, and its best results matched the quality of human expert labels.  Furthermore, researchers explored PILE's ability to distill labels for various learning objectives, such as math and reading, and found that it could produce high-quality labels for each objective independently.  A comprehensive technical report on PILE is available at https://public.iai.gov/mLE/distillation/

The current research into the nature of dark matter is intensively ongoing, with various experimental and theoretical probes being employed to uncover the mysterious substance. A previously unexplored option suggests that ultra-light bosonic dark matter, weighing as little as $\sim 10^{-23}$eV, might be indentified through its impact on laboratory measurements of nuclear quadrupole interactions. This could provide insight into the matter at a testing range of $\sim$10-1000 micrometers. This research calculates the influence of ultra-light bosonic dark matter on the measured frequency shifts and damping rates of optical fibers, and proposes a viable strategy for distinguishing between different dark matter models using fiber network measurements. This experiment could ultimately reveal the properties of the dark matter, or set a stringent limit on its mass.

This research investigates the uniqueness of solutions to basis pursuit in a continuous setting. By proving that basis pursuit has a distinct and unique solution for any given basis and measurement functions, we resolve a longstanding open issue initially posed by Efromovich (1990). The study further demonstrates that under certain conditions, basis pursuit can be smoothly perturbed to yield a precise recovery of the target function, even in the presence of noisy measurements.

P4 has gained acceptance as a programming language for configurable switch hardware, allowing researchers and developers to create intricate packet-processing programs. However, the language's syntax and implementation are complex, making it difficult to translate P4 programs into hardware-compatible code. This complexity stems from the challenges of mapping abstract P4 syntax to concrete switch instructions, considering factors like register allocation, table selection, and instruction embedding. A P4 translator is needed to render programs executable on real-world switches, but the translation process involves numerous optimizations and compromises to achieve this functionality. A comprehensive framework for P4 translation is introduced, addressing issues like hardware compatibility, register allocation, and table placement. The proposed framework utilizes graph theory and heuristics for register allocation and table placement, with support for multiple optimization strategies and a detailed explanation of the compilation framework and its components. The accompanying code provides a clear approach to P4 translation, facilitating the compilation of P4 programs into hardware-compatible code.

This study focuses on discretising the vector conveyance equation using the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas finite elements and aims to optimize spatial discretisation error. To achieve this, two novel penalty parameters are introduced in the boundary conditions, which enable us to systematically analyze the error in approximation. This involves investigating the $L^2$ error in both space and time, with the ultimate goal being to derive a time step restriction that will result in $O(T^{-1/2})$ convergence. Furthermore, our analysis confirms that the spatial error is $O(h^{-1/2})$, indicating that conveyance acts as a $H^{-1/2}$-stabilising mechanism. To realise the optimal $O(T^{-1/2})$ time step restriction, we devised a iterative solution strategy consisting of two stages: a $H^1$-stabilised or "weak" formulation step, followed by a penalty penalty step. In practical terms, realising the optimal $O(T^{-1/2})$ time step restriction simply requires adopting a two-stage iterative solution method.

Federated Learning aims to achieve data protection through 'deletion' by keeping sensitive data localized, yet it may fail in achieving 'justice' as data is still compromised during federated averaging. This paper explores two concepts, data justice and secure code, using the framework of differential privacy. It proposes a new formula for federated averaging that incorporates an adjustable safety margin and provides a framework for choosing the optimal safety margin. This results in two new algorithms: Justice-FedAvg and Encrypted-FedAvg, which prioritize data protection over performance and security over performance, respectively. Justice-FedAvg offers a flexible solution that can be tailored to various ethical requirements, while Encrypted-FedAvg is a secure alternative to traditional FedAvg. The performance of both algorithms is evaluated on MNIST and CIFAR10 using various ethical specifications.

The investigation for the $B_c^*$ meson, specifically its $\mathrm{B_c^*(2S)}$ state,
has been investigated by analyzing energy differences between low-lying $\mathrm{B_c^+}$ states.
These analyses used quantum chromodynamics simulations, revealing a previously undiscovered state
at around 2.63 GeV, corresponding to the $\mathrm{B_c^+}(2S)$ meson, which is consistent
with observations from LHCb experiments. In this study, we introduced three new observables
related to rare decays, facilitating $\mathrm{B_c^+}(2S)$ detection, without which
detection would be impossible. A thorough discussion on recent experiments and potential future research
has also been included.

Not all problems that arise from measuring data can be modeled by a single linear equation. Some difficulties are caused by random factors, such as noise, that can be filtered out, but others result from inherent properties of the measured signal, such as discontinuities or non-linear patterns. In such cases, the need arises for specialized methods to accurately calculate the desired parameters. This study presents an original non-linear estimation technique, Continuous-Phase Runge-Kutta, that can handle various types of differential problems, including those influenced by measurement noise. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through applications to model signals with broken derivatives and nonlinear trajectories, often found in real-world data.

This research introduces an innovative technique for parallel training deep neural networks using model parallelism. We have developed an evaluator-based model parallel training framework that separates the computation of neural networks into multiple segments and assigns each to a different device. Our key contribution lies in the introduction of regional evaluators, which are responsible for meshing the computed node values. We have created a novel communication protocol that consolidates the values of adjacent nodes through a mathematical transformation. This allows data exchange between devices only at the boundaries, minimizing communication traffic and enhancing system efficiency. Our model, which can be applied to various neural networks, is versatile and user-friendly. We have conducted comprehensive experiments on ResNet-101, MobileNetV2, and SeNet-154 using a multi-GPU platform. The results demonstrate that our technique can achieve optimal performance within a single machine, and a reasonable speed-up with minimal computational overhead.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart.  A two-dimensional system featuring Wada basins was recently found to survive minimal perturbations.  This study investigates the impact of a three-dimensional generalization of this system, wherein the basins of Wada transform into feeble dissipative sets associated with compact regular escape trajectories.  Unlike two-dimensional Wada basins, these suffer from an absence of universality, instead experiencing enhancement due to a variety of mechanisms including a mechanism producing 'whirlpools'.  A three-dimensional generalization of this 'whirlpool' mechanism amplifies the basins of Wada.

Theories beyond the standard model frequently propose the existence of sub-GeV bosons, which could be detected through unique tastes rather than durable signatures. Current experimental constraints, however, limit the potential for detection by requiring tastes that manifest in a highly unstable state. We present a new idea suggesting that these bosons could have different properties in various taste configurations, both stable and unstable. This concept is implemented by a simple model involving an $SU(N)$ symmetry, offering two forms of taste alchemy and a potential for further exploration in nuclear physics and cosmology.

In daily life, people commonly refer to short video segments as "clips." These clips are frequently used in various applications, including opera and dance footage. The challenge of recognizing activities within these clips is more complex than usual due to several factors. Firstly, the duration of each clip is limited, making it harder for models to focus. Secondly, the distribution of data is uneven, leading to fewer high-quality examples for training. To overcome these difficulties, we developed a new technique called Focus Network, consisting of multiple layers that gradually increase in resolution and focus, similar to how the human brain processes information. We also created a data augmentation method to improve model performance by combining training with labeled clips and synthetic data. The model's effectiveness was demonstrated through rigorous testing on various datasets, including Sunset, WildLifeCam-Challenge, and Kinetics actions. Our technique outperformed existing methods on Sunset and WildLifeCam-Challenge datasets.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship hypothesis in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering may offer insights into the universe's initial phases. Analyzing the Scattering Amplitude and System's Energy, researchers find that large negative surface gravities can result from scalar field interactions, which could imply a violation of the cosmic censorship hypothesis under testing. Nevertheless, further investigation via Poincaré recurrence relates the cosmic censorship hypothesis to the laws of thermodynamics, revealing that cosmic censorship's non-violation is directly tied to the second law of thermodynamics and, consequently, tied to the non-existence of spontaneous surface gravity change. Since surface gravity change represents a measure of black hole instability, non-existence of such instances validates the cosmic censorship hypothesis, thereby confirming black hole stability. Moreover, researchers have found that the cosmological constant's minima are equilibrium positions, marking a significant relationship between the universe's initial phases and thermodynamic equilibrium. Finally, researchers have observed that the universe's initial phases, characterized by the cosmological constant's minima as thermodynamic equilibrium, are consistent with the hypothesis that the universe's initial phases began as thermodynamic equilibrium systems.

This article will examine the primary stages of star formation, focusing on how stars are created and how their formation is regulated. It will also explore how the theoretical concepts developed during this process are reconciled with observational findings.

This paper proposes a new method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, using Nested Sampling. The method assigns more sampling effort to areas of greater relevance, allowing for calculation of entropy as a weighted average of log-probabilities. The approach can easily incorporate prior knowledge incorporated into the probability distribution being calculated. The paper demonstrates the method's effectiveness with mutual information estimates and suggests possible adaptations for other uncertainty metrics.

A particular type of first-order hyperbolic PDE will be examined, along with its corresponding Riemann problem, in a highly irregular domain. Solutions to this problem will be shown to be weakly continuous with respect to measure, and we will demonstrate the non-uniqueness of solutions by constructing an infinite number of diverse weakly continuous measure-valued solutions, each corresponding to a different initial condition. These solutions can be represented as a feeble limit of a sequence of solutions to approximated problems with smooth solutions and a finite number of shocks.

Cybersecurity threats to IoT devices are rapidly evolving, leading to increasingly complex network assaults, which necessitate rapid detection and response to prevent significant damage to resources. However, traditional intrusion detection systems are often insufficient, prompting a need for more effective solutions. This paper introduces NBcoded, a novel scheme that utilizes machine learning to classify network assaults in IoT environments. NBcoded leverages a neural network and Naive Bayes model to increase assault recognition accuracy, simplifying implementation and reducing computational demands on resource-constrained devices. Theoretical foundations and simulations validate the proposed approach, highlighting its efficiency and reliability in real-world scenarios.

Given a solvable group G and a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of G, we investigate the number of group homomorphisms from $P$ to the multiplicative group of a finite field $GF(q)$, where the prime $p$ is less than or equal to $q$. We provide a formula that expresses the count of these homomorphisms as a product of factors, where the first factor is the order of $P$, and the remaining factors are integers defined by $G$ and $p$. We derive a recursive formula to compute these integrals, which subsequently allows us to obtain a closed-form expression for the count of group homomorphisms by utilizing classical results from the theory of linear difference equations. We also obtain a direct computation of the count, which further enables us to establish a connection with the $p$-rank of $G$, where the count of homomorphisms is shown to be a product of factors, where the first factor is the order of $P$, and the remaining factors are power functions of $q$, where the exponents are determined by the $p$-rank of $G$.

Plant movement detection through analysis of temporal image sequences has been the focus of ongoing research in computational biology. This study proposes an innovative framework for detecting plant movement within a temporal image series. The proposed method utilizes image processing and machine learning techniques to extract subtle plant movements, enabling researchers to assess health and detect pathogens more accurately. Evaluation of the approach revealed promising results, demonstrating its ability to detect even minimal movement, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

Electrical energy networks undergo temporary disruptions due to excessive load or network damage. This research employs a quantum-informed algorithm to minimize these disruptions by optimizing load distribution. A comparison with classical counterparts shows that the quantum-based approach leads to reduced communication overhead and faster convergence. Furthermore, the quantum method can efficiently resolve contingency problems that classical methods struggle with.

Revealing the underlying physics of a system through data analysis involves
selecting an appropriate model that best explains the observed data. In
phenomenological investigations, inconsistencies in physics are identified when
different theories predict data outcomes differently. Notably, the process of
model selection incorporates inherent uncertainties and limitations, prompting
the question of whether inaccuracies in model prediction are an inconsistency of
the model or the observer. In this study, concepts from cognitive relativity and
information theory are explored to clarify this confusion, focusing on how
inconsistencies in prediction relate to uncertainties in measurement and
relevance uncertainty. We examine two scenarios: (i) predictions based on same
or different models, and (ii) comparisons with predictions made by other
observers. Furthermore, we examine how relevance uncertainty affects the choice
of model and whether previous models were inadequate. In situations where
relevance uncertainty exists, we propose that non-uniqueness in prediction does
not constitute an inconsistency in physics. However, when relevance uncertainty
can be eliminated, inconsistencies in physics are identified when predictions
differ based on various models considered relevant. Additionally, we investigate
the possibility of existing inconsistencies in physics that cannot be resolved by
further data refinement. In such cases, further experimentation is necessary to
eliminate uncertainty in measurement and potentially new, relevant theories
that can explain the observed data.

A comprehensive search for persistent, long-lasting, charged particles is presented, utilizing the ATLAS detector's full dataset collected from the 2015 to 2018 $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, along with searches for hypothetical particles models and other exotic phenomena. The data amount to 139 fb$^{-1}$ of collision data. The search focuses on charged particles that persist for tens of millimeters and exhibit significant energy loss due to ionization. No evidence for any unusual activity is observed, and upper limits are established for the 2015-2018 data, ranging from 86 to 875 times that of the standard QCD prediction, depending on the parameters and models tested. The theoretical models explored include massive $W'$ bosons, R-higgs bosons, Higgs boson interactions with scalar dark matter, and other processes such as quarkino states and Jordan frames where the Higgs field acts as, but is not, a Majoron in a left-right symmetric model.

We have developed a design of near-unity coherence and high photon collection efficiency in ridge waveguide-based, on-chip single-photon generators using a silicon platform. The design features a modified single-photon router architecture with an adjustable fractional beta parameter in the hybrid microring-substrate modegap cavity. This parameter, influencing the microring's resonance condition, can be manipulated through cavity-substrate gap or radius adjustment without altering the cavity's phonon structure. Consequently, this versatility enables near-unity coherence among the device's optical modes, which is crucial for achieving high photon collection efficiency and minimizing losses in single-photon circuits. Furthermore, our findings can be expanded to other single-photon circuits, such as quantum frequency converters and single-photon switches, to optimize their performance.

Neutron spin flip and inelastic scattering experiments were conducted on
high-field spin ice materials, specifically on principles of $H$ and $D$ with
various magnetic field applications, ranging from 0 to 14 Tesla. The results from
these experiments were compared to simulations using a 3D random flux line model
to better understand the dynamics behind a phenomenon known as boson summit, a
concept originating from a theory describing high-field spin ice. The presence of
boson summit was confirmed through analysis of the wave number and energy
spectrum of excitions, which were found to follow a 1/d^2 law, and the associated
wave number spectrum of spin polarizations that exhibits a 1/d law. The application
of external magnetic fields in these experiments led to a shift in the energy
spectrum of excitions towards higher energies, resulting in a decrease in intensity. 
The intensity of this shift increased with fields beyond 10 Tesla, suggesting a
relationship between field strength and boson summit intensity. The relationship
between boson summit intensity and field strength was found to be consistent with
predictions from 3D random flux line model, which was also used to explain the
observed shift in the wave number spectrum of excitions, which can be attributed to
a increase in summit density.

Particle physics is reliant on theoretical models, which involve using mathematical equations to predict outcomes. Certain complex mathematical equations, known as Feynman integrals, are necessary for these models but are difficult to solve due to their complex nature. Advances in computational methods and composable design enable the efficient calculation of these integrals, allowing for more precise predictions in physics. This leads to improved understanding, accurate model validation, and enhanced analysis in physics. This method is particularly beneficial for analyzing phenomena at various scales and in diverse environments. Several key case studies, such as top quark analysis, Higgs boson investigation, and precision calculations at LHC and future colliders, will be examined to illustrate its practical significance.

The transmission of waves in disordered media can be described using absorbing channels, where channels are classified as direct or indirect based on their connection to a designated energy source. A fundamental theory relating to conservative systems revealed that all incoming energy is accounted for by summing totals from individual channels. This research expands upon this idea to non-conservative systems by demonstrating that total energy absorption in disordered systems can be expressed as a combination of channel contributions from direct and indirect channels. Additionally, this study confirms that total energy absorbed through a specific interface cannot exceed the energy introduced through that interface.

Researchers have studied the outer spiral limbs of galaxies using newly acquired data from the Integrated Galactic Field module on board the Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy. A keystone 3-kiloparsec arc, visible in infrared, has long been obscured in the Milky Way by dust, hiding its spiral structure. This arc, comprising the most distant features in the galaxy's central regions, has been found to exhibit distinct rotational phases. Through spatial and temporal analysis, researchers have uncovered evidence of two distinct spiral arms. Furthermore, models indicate that these arcs are mostly composed of cold molecular clouds. It's suggested that these clouds originated in localized star-forming regions and were deposited on the arc shape as the galaxy rotated. It's proposed that similar cloud formations may be present in other spiral galaxies, but are yet to be detected.

This study investigates variety in multi-solution optimization by optimizing multiple objectives at once to generate a set of varied solutions. We're looking to understand how different optimization algorithms affect solution variety in contrast to searching for diverse solutions one objective at a time. Our test cases demonstrate that optimizing all objectives simultaneously can lead to more varied outcomes, although the impact on overall diversity depends on various factors. A prominent role is played by solution crowding, the tendency of certain multi-objective algorithms to crowd solutions with similar attributes, reducing the range of experienced values and thus diversity potential. To gauge solution diversity, we created a generic assessment framework that can be applied to a range of optimization strategies, including both classic methods and more innovative approaches. Our analysis offers new insights to optimize both performance and diversity when optimizing multiple objectives at once.

We're investigating a three-dimensional stable house of three housemates with unique preference lists and finding that under a specific structure of these lists, the scenario is equivalent to a two-dimensional stable marriage with preferences that vary linearly. To demonstrate our findings, we first break down the one-dimensional stable housemate problem into a linear preference marriage problem, and then apply this transformation to the two-dimensional case to obtain our result.

A quantitative description of how valleys in two-dimensional materials move around and change has been figured out using sophisticated mathematical equations that take into account how electrons interact with each other and with the underlying lattice. This understanding is crucial for making more accurate predictions about how valleys in such materials move around and change, which is important for the development of new technologies that rely on valleys. Based on this, a formula has been developed to make predictions about how valleys in such materials move around and change when there are different levels of interaction between electrons and the underlying lattice. This was verified by comparing the predictions with experimental data from real-life experiments on a particular type of material called hBN. This research also showed that taking into account new mechanisms of electron-lattice interaction can explain the shift in the Hall effect that has been observed in experiments.

This research introduces a new type of cloud that belongs to the Gromov-Hausdorff category, consisting of all possible Gromov-Hausdorff approximations of a given category. We present two primary forms of these clouds: the 'whole cloud' that includes all Gromov-Hausdorff approximations and a more compact 'core cloud' obtained by truncating the periphery of the whole cloud. Additionally, we define and study a subset of these clouds known as 'central clouds', derived from approximations with minimal distortion. We demonstrate that the structure of central clouds is straightforward, whereas the whole cloud exhibits greater complexity. Moreover, we find that the surface of the core cloud develops a Sierpinski carpet-like pattern as the scale approaches a certain limit.

This research introduces a designed microstrip patch antenna operating in the mm-Wave range. The proposed antenna features a maximum bandwidth of 7.32 GHz and a wide angular range of 60 degrees. Built with a simplified structure consisting of microstrip feed and parasitic patches, this antenna demonstrates excellent matching with a return loss of -38.9 dB and 94% efficiency across its bandwidth. The calculated gain and efficiency are 6.9 dBi and 99%, respectively. Furthermore, the antenna meets the requirements of being broadband, wide-angle, and compact (45 mm x 45 mm), making it suitable for integration into array antennas and wireless communication devices operating in the mm-Wave band.

As quantum processors mature, they face challenges stemming from hardware errors, memory limitations, and management complexity. To overcome these issues, we're developing an autonomous quantum circuit execution system utilizing reinforcement learning-based coding, aiming to provide fault-resilient computation directly in the quantum processor's programming language. This system leverages the coder's intentions to minimize resource usage, ensuring optimal output quality. Our coder employs policy-based reinforcement learning to make execution-related decisions, while the emitter acts as a fault-introducing surrogate to gather essential knowledge for stable circuit creation. Without requiring introductory knowledge of coding, the coder optimizes circuit creation, leading to substantial reductions in qubit regulation, gate, and sequence errors. Furthermore, the coder's capabilities extend to detecting and fixing faulty quantum circuits. Our findings demonstrate that this coder successfully creates stable quantum circuits, effectively managing execution, and outperforming current industry standards introduced by our research colleagues.

Quantum-enhanced metrology (QEM) can offer significant advantages over classical methods by utilizing carefully engineered quantum states and precise control of quantum interactions. Theoretical studies have revealed that specific double-cavity networks can perform precision measurements of certain target parameters with exceptionally high sensitivity, surpassing conventional limits by a factor of $10^{2N}$, where $N$ represents the number of paired cavities. The proposed quantum metrology scheme relies on strategically combining optical modes of varying frequencies and degrees of freedom, as well as applying intelligent measurements to maximize the information extracted from the system. Notably, despite being prone to losses, this method can still outdo traditional techniques by a factor of around $100. The proposed system could be implemented using current technological capabilities and is expected to offer notably improved precision in measuring parameters such as the phase shift and beam splitting ratio.

Research on the collisions of 200 GeV Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au at RHIC has been conducted to examine jet-medium interactions, specifically how low-energy photons form in these events, and how they correlate with hadrons. The analysis of direct photon-hadron correlations near the photon's direction of travel has yielded initial findings that may indicate suppressed hadron yields at large angles and hadron yields that are paired with the photons, when compared to $d$$+$Au collisions. The suppression of hadron yields at large angles to the photon's direction of travel suggests that jets produced in these events lose energy and shift direction due to interactions with the Au+Au medium, while suppressed yields of hadron pairs aligned with the photons may indicate cold nuclear matter effects, and/or energy taken by the jets due to interactions with the Au+Au medium. The analysis of these photon-hadron correlations provides insights into jet-medium interactions and cold nuclear matter effects, and may offer insight into how low-energy photons form in these events.

Researchers have made substantial progress in developing quantum computers that can efficiently solve complex problems. However, the development of quantum computers that can handle complex systems with numerous interacting particles remains a major challenge. This issue remains particularly prevalent in the study of fermionic systems found in nature. To mitigate this limitation, our research proposes a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach. This method utilizes a quantum computer that leverages a continuous wave function, analog quantum processing, and qumonics (quantum monolithic circuits) to create an equivalent quantum state. The proposed hybrid approach enables the simulation of fermionic systems by mimicking the fermionic creation and annihilation operators, and we demonstrate its efficacy in the example of the fermionic hydrogen atom. This method shows great potential for efficiently simulating complex fermionic systems.

A prominent issue in machine learning has come to be known as the optimization-generalization disparity, which refers to the phenomenon where machine learning models excel in optimization but severely underperform in real-world applications. In this study, researchers reframe this problem as a process of discovering attributes from existing data and demonstrate that wealthy attributes resolve the optimization-generalization paradox. Enriched attributes that are extracted from the target dataset are shown to significantly enhance a model's real-world performance, despite potentially hindering its optimization performance. Additionally, researchers present a novel algorithm called Wealthy Attribute Finder (WAF) that systematically identifies and selects attributes with the potential to improve real-world results. To validate the efficacy of WAF, researchers conducted comprehensive experiments on 7 open-source datasets from various domains and found that the models trained with attributes from WAF generalizable performance surpass that of the baseline models by 26.3%, while also showing 18.3% less overfitting.

The use of structured illumination in 3D imaging techniques has become increasingly common, but its application in tissue has been hindered by the low contrast produced by its inherent speckle pattern. This limitation has made 3D imaging in tissue inhospitable to structured illumination techniques. However, the advent of fast and high-resolution spatial light modulators has opened the door for a novel solution. By employing an algorithm-driven approach, we can leverage a programmable SLM to generate multiple low-contrast patterns simultaneously, effectively converting a dual-objective imaging challenge into a feasible task. This concept can be extended to control the formation of multiple three-dimensional objects through the iterative use of various phase patterns displayed on the SLM. Our proposed framework, designed for a tandem system consisting of an SLM and a camera, enables the creation of multiple three-dimensional objects with a high signal-to-noise ratio by collectively analyzing the images captured during the imaging process. This capability was successfully demonstrated in our experiments, where we used the proposed framework to construct two three-dimensional objects with intricate structures. Our results indicate that this approach can produce images with a resolution of approximately 5.7 micrometers, representing a significant improvement over current methods.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work aims to establish a theoretical framework linking treatment guidelines' robustness to their performance, making them less susceptible to changes in the data distribution. To achieve this, we developed a concept for distributional robustness rooted in information theory, then identified practical bounds on treatment effectiveness relative to optimal outcomes, factoring in varying data distributions. Although the limits of this theoretical framework are narrow, they represent a theoretical baseline for guiding treatments in real-world scenarios. To improve these theoretical limitations, future research should focus on refining the proposed robustness measure and relaxing associated constraints.

Monolithic 64-channel CMOS sensors featuring 25 $\mu$m hammerhead structures, 30 $\mu$m disk sensors, and 40 $\mu$m rectangular sensitive areas are presented from an CCSDS-compliant CLICTD technology, comprising five high-resistivity options. The options include 100 mm p-type wafers made from silicon, as well as 100 mm insulating substrates made from silicon-on-insulator (SOI), 100 mm p-type epitaxial wafers, 150 mm p-type wafers, and 150 mm SOI wafers. The goal is to determine the best choice for new sensor developments, leveraging the monolithic collection-electrode technology. The study includes the investigation of sensor function, electrical properties, radiation sensitivity, and charge collection capabilities across various sensor thicknesses and substrate options.

A new development in adaptive optics (AO) technology is the Atmospheric Self-Coherent Camera (ASCC), an unconventional approach that employs interference-pattern-detecting capabilities, enabling the detection of the residual phase error in the optical path. This approach bypasses the need for an additional laser, making it more accessible, and has successfully been tested in various environments - from the laboratory to space - with impressive results, including the detection of phase errors, the prediction of the ASCC signal's statistical properties, and the successful use of the ASCC signal in guiding an AO system. This technique has now been successfully implemented on the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Testbed (SC-EAOT) with remarkable results, including the confirmation of the ASCC signal's spatial scale and the achievement of wavefront residuals close to the theoretical limit.

This study examines two variants of the Merino-Cchusseau model, specifically its Cox-Ingersoll and Hull-White variants, and suggests implementing a novel interest rate model, the deterministic-shift enhanced CIR model. The Cox-Ingersoll and Merino-Cchusseau models are established frameworks, but this new model, however, lacks a well-documented theoretical foundation in an unfavorable interest rate environment. Our focus is on the theoretical aspects of this new model, specifically the existence and uniqueness of its differential equation, as well as the probability measure's determination in an unfavorable interest rate setting. Additionally, this study investigates the asymptotic behavior of the model's distribution and its likelihood function. To establish a unfavorable interest rate framework, this study turns to Heston's characteristic function method and applies Harvey's non-traditional approach for probability measure determination. The unfavorable interest rate setting in this study is in line with the multifactorization principle, specifically Merino and Saxo Institute's framework.

Research into DUNE's capability to find out about its potential to detect sterile neutrinos is being investigated. By capturing neutrino data from atmospheric source, Kamiokande and DUNE can measure the influence of sterile neutrinos. This study assesses the likelihood of detecting sterile neutrinos at DUNE using the near detector, assuming various assumptions about the rate of sterile neutrino creation in the atmosphere. It reveals that, under most scenarios, DUNE has a high potential to accurately measure this process, albeit with a lower probability than what can be measured at the far detector. This study demonstrates that the near and far detectors contribute equally to precision measurements of certain aspects of neutrino interaction processes. Furthermore, the near and far detectors have distinct advantages in furthering understanding of two distinct aspects of neutrino physics.

Meta-analysts often encounter inconsistent research results, which can be resolved by conducting a meta-analysis to produce reliable estimates of the mean treatment effects across multiple studies. However, our meta-analytic estimates may lack precision due to the limited sample sizes available. To improve accuracy, researchers often incorporate prior knowledge into their estimates, but conventional methods rarely utilize individual study data beyond its minimum information. In this research, we introduce novel cluster-stable estimators capable of harnessing all available data, prior knowledge, and between-study variability. Our estimators range from simple to complex forms, each suitable for various scenarios, from which we select the most appropriate model for bivariate mixed-effects meta-analyses. To evaluate our method, both simulated and real-world data are used to demonstrate its superiority in estimating treatment effects, confidence intervals, and model parameters. Furthermore, all necessary software to reproduce our results can be accessed through the publicly available R package "MetaBayes".

This study proposes a novel integration method for simulating multiphase flows at the particle level, accommodating various collision times between particles. The method leverages time steps that can be chosen independently of particle sizes, allowing for efficient simulation calculations. The method was validated through a series of benchmarks, including collisions between particles, particles and walls, and particles and fluids. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the application of the method in modeling a particle suspended in a fluid and colliding with a wall, while also capturing the continuous fluid flow around the particle.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking phenomenon is essential to understanding its mechanism. Our study proposes that the source of emission comes from unbalanced gravitational force, which can be extracted and represented mathematically using the Einstein tensor, particularly in the scenario of an eternal black hole. Additionally, our findings also apply to the case of an eternal black/white hole dual system, where we interpret the radiation as originating from states of high energy density in the white hole region, which cannot be accessed causally. Our model demonstrates how Hawking radiation can be associated with the dynamic process of an unstable black/white hole system, where energy is conserved globally but individual components may appear to lose mass due to unbalanced gravitational interactions.

High-density nuclear matter is created at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) through collisions with large relativistic velocities, where the color multiplicity of partons in the nuclei's transverse plane is examined using the color dipole model at medium saturation point. By accounting for parton lateral momentum disparities, this study matches measured data with previous observations of nuclear modifications, particularly at the LHC energy regime, which showed significant differences in momentum distributions between central and peripheral regions. Various nuclear state models were explored, including purely statistical models that consider parton thermalization in the transverse plane. However, only the quark gelation model, which incorporates non-thermal parton states with an increased maximum lateral momentum, successfully explains the color dipole cross-section data at the LHC energy domain.

This article presents whole number solutions for the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ by extending the method in an earlier paper by Wechsler and Jackson. Initially, the article establishes certain constraints on whole number values of $a$ and $b$ such that their combination meets the condition that the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored into the product of two other expressions, further proving additional limitations on these whole number values. Notably, it is shown that any whole number solution to this equation must have both $a$ and $b$ relatively prime to 7. By integrating the results from an earlier paper by Lay, the article presents a general whole number solution for the given equation, refining the scope of this solution from the broad category of relatively prime whole numbers to specifically whole numbers. Finally, the article validates its whole number solution through extensive case analysis involving the various possible values of $n$ and further affirms that any whole number solution to this equation must have both $a$ and $b$ relatively prime to 7.

The behavior of a liquid jet that enters a channel occupied by the same fluid is investigated using experimental and numerical methods. When the jet's influence extends beyond its initial range, it creates a mobile liquid front that interacts with the surrounding air in the channel. This study specifically examines how this liquid front behaves when it encounters a sudden increase in the cross-sectional area of the channel. Our findings show that the deceleration of the liquid jet at this point causes it to break up into smaller droplets, creating instability. This mode of instability is similar to that observed in a pendant droplet shedding process, and can be explained by a critical change in the liquid's velocity and a corresponding increase in pressure. Additionally, we have conducted simulations using the Volume Of Fluid method to reproduce the experimental results and validate the findings.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on reliable storage to function properly, especially since crashes during write operations can lead to data corruption. In real-world scenarios, even the most advanced non-volatile storage solutions experience crashes at around one failure every 220 years. These events, though extremely rare, pose significant risks, including data loss and system disruptions. Researchers have developed new approaches, such as check-pointing and robust write algorithms, to mitigate these issues, but they come with their own drawbacks, like performance slowdowns and increased latency. A more direct solution involves algorithm-guided crash reliability, which provides guarantees based on specific failure probabilities associated with each write algorithm. By integrating crash reliability into existing storage systems, developers can ensure data integrity and choose from various trade-off points between performance, latency, and the likelihood of data corruption. In our study, we demonstrate how to integrate this new crash reliability framework into existing storage systems, while also presenting a number of storage algorithms that offer various performance, latency, and reliability trade-offs.

In the context of information systems, hierarchies are utilized to streamline the processing and analysis of data. For example, in business information systems, product categories can be grouped into higher-level categories such as "electronics," which can further be categorized into sub-categories like smartphones and televisions. The concept of hierarchy is crucial in database design, cartography, and knowledge structure management, among other fields. This study proposes a set of rules for defining hierarchies within information systems and establishes a framework for identifying and constructing hierarchies through data analysis. The paper also introduces a novel method for expanding upon existing hierarchies, enabling researchers to replicate and build upon one another's work. This method involves using data attributes and relationships to create new hierarchies, which can be applied to both relational databases and knowledge graphs. A demonstration of this approach is provided using the DBLP dataset.

Recent research proposed a statistical model, known as the Flux-driven Three-Body Problem, to address the daunting task of predicting outcomes in complex systems with varied interactions. Despite initial skepticism due to its unorthodox nature, the statistical nature of its predictions aligns with historical estimates. To validate this approach, we evaluated its performance in a study, investigating the following questions: First, does the statistical model accurately forecast outcomes in a diverse set of systems? Second, what benefits does it offer compared to traditional numerical integration methods? Our analysis reveals that, surprisingly, numerical integration often fails to accurately predict long-term behavior, whereas the statistical model excels in those instances. Conversely, in systems where numerical integration is feasible, the statistical model's unique features yield no significant advantage. Our findings suggest that the statistical model may serve as a valuable tool for forecasting outcomes in complex systems, particularly those that numerical integration cannot reliably handle.

Measurements of the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ production in PbPb collisions at 5.02 TeV have been carried out to assess the suppression of these charmonium states in heavy-ion collisions. The assessment includes a comparison of the immediate (prompt) and non-immediate (delayed) production of these states. The analysis is based on data from the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS experiments. The LHC data are combined with calculations from NRQCD to determine if they match the predicted immediate production rates. The combined results indicate that, except for a disparity at the lowest $p_T$, the data are in line with the predicted immediate production rates. The suppression of these charmonium states is compared to the predicted levels of suppression based on the initial temperatures of 350 and 500 MeV. The study shows that, in the case of $J/\psi$, the suppression based on the initial temperature of 350 MeV does not exceed the observed suppression by more than 50%. However, the suppression based on the initial temperature of 500 MeV exceeds the observed suppression by more than 50%. The suppression of $\psi(2S)$ states is more pronounced than that of $J/\psi$ states at the same temperature. The observed $\psi(2S)$ suppression exceeds the predicted suppression based on the initial temperature of 350 MeV by as much as 80% and the suppression based on the initial temperature of

Mathematics is being increasingly viewed as a categorical concept, where properties and relationships are categorised to encompass a broader range of mathematical structures. This paper proposes a basic logical framework that incorporates categorical principles, allowing for the representation of abstract algebraic properties through the use of categories with additional constitutive elements, where equivalence classes and operations are defined constitutionally. This framework enables reasoning about partial operations in a systematic way, facilitating the application of categorical reasoning methods.

One of the key components of bug detection tools is the test scenario generation module, which identifies a subset of predefined scenarios tailored to uncover specific bugs within a program. This selection process involves analyzing a program's execution history, marked with bug indicators, to pick the most relevant scenarios. Since each program is distinct, there's currently a lack of standardized bug detection frameworks, making it challenging to apply existing algorithms across different software without significant modifications. To enhance the efficiency of bug detection frameworks, we introduce a parallelized algorithm for test scenario selection, leveraging Unique Value Decomposition, to optimize scenario selection on large datasets. This implementation is versatile and can be applied to various bug detection frameworks with minimal adjustments, improving its overall performance.

Individuals who exhibit suicidal behavior pose a significant challenge to mental health care systems, requiring precise identification and effective intervention to prevent tragic outcomes. Previous studies have established that individuals who are likely to suicide have particular characteristics, such as previous suicide attempts, hospitalizations, and diagnoses. To develop an effective strategy for identifying high-risk suicidal individuals, we have created a comprehensive framework that integrates data from multiple sources in a sequential manner. By testing this framework on a real-world dataset derived from the Electronic Health Record, we have obtained outstanding results, with an AUC of 0.9426 for suicide risk prediction. Furthermore, by analyzing the performance of various model components and case studies, we have gained insights into the framework's functionality and its potential to improve suicide prevention.

Our research reports a definitive detection of circular polarization within a specific energy range in X-rays emitted from Cassiopeia A. Utilizing the IXPE, we analyzed 11 days' worth of data and discovered polarization levels amounting to $0.43 \pm 0.13$ at $5\sigma$ confidence, with an associated 95% error margin. This finding aligns with the expectation that synchrotron radiation, produced by electrons interacting with magnetic fields in the supernova remnant's reverse shock, gives rise to the observed polarization. Furthermore, our analysis set an upper limit of $2 \times 10^{-8}$ on linear polarization in X-rays emitted by Cas A.

Consider a set $\Sigma$ consisting of $n$ distinct elements, with the property that the sum $S$ can be expressed as a unique combination of those elements. Erdos posed the question as to how large $\sigma(n)$ needs to be for such a set $\Sigma$ to exist, with $\sigma(n)$ representing the total number of possible sums that can be formed using the elements of $\Sigma$. This paper explores modified versions of Erdos's original conjecture, including scenarios where the set $\Sigma$ is comprised of nonnegative integers, and another where the sum $S$ is restricted to be greater than the size of $\Sigma$.

In astrophysics, sound wave equations in stars are crucial for sound speed determination. However, Adams and Allen in 2009 discovered adiabatic sound speed to be inconsistent with barotropic sound speed in general relativistic compact stars. We find that the cause of this incoherence lies in the adiabatic sound speed definition and density variations. We provide a mathematical expression for barotropic sound speed that is applicable to all types of fluid and relativistic or non-relativistic energy conditions. Using a detailed example in dense stellar substance with "nucleon" "quark" matter and "quark" matter with "strange" phase, we demonstrate how the equation for barotropic sound speed behaves in different matter phases. We also calculate the adiabatic sound speed in stellar matter cross-sections and plot them against density and temperature, showcasing how the equation for barotropic sound speed behaves in different matter phases.

This study explores the effect of camera system compression and data shift on the Fock space in a depth-of-field simulation. To achieve this, we examined the relationship between photon phase and spatial distribution. Leveraging the connection between the Wigner function and the joint spectral density, we were able to derive a expression that relates the Wigner function to the joint spectral density, enabling us to investigate how camera system parameters influence the Fock space. By compressing the Fock space, we found that the final spectral density exhibits symmetry about its center, and as the level of compression increases, the spectral density becomes broader. A decrease in the level of compression results in the emergence of distinct quanta in the spectral density. Introducing a data shift leads to the splitting of the compressed Fock space into two separate regions. Furthermore, we identified a relationship between the amount of compression and the phase of photons in each region.

This research aims to leverage skeletal representation for the extraction of statistical insights into the complex interfaces formed between gas and liquid during non-reacting two-phase flows. By defining the interface through a weighted surface, we can calculate its skeletal structure, which comprises points representing the surface's local convexity and concavity. These skeletal points group nearby points together, enabling the assignment of an orientation to each point based on a normal vector. Subsequent sectioning of the skeletal structure by planes allows for the examination of cross-sections, ultimately leading to the characterization of interface morphology. Our method has been successfully tested using real numerical data from simulations of air bubbles in a fluid and a further comparison with experimental X-ray imaging data revealed a strong correspondence between the extracted skeletal structure and the observed structures. We found that our skeletal representation can accurately reproduce the overall skeletal structure, detail, and organization of the interface, presenting a promising approach for generalization to detecting three-dimensional interfaces. Additionally, further development is planned to utilize skeletal points for the quantification of interface characteristics such as curvature and area.

Researchers propose a novel virus model that exhibits intrinsic rolling motion during membrane traversal. This proposal is grounded in real-world evidence, including cryo-electron microscopy images of herpes simplex virus 1. By developing a finite-element method to analyze the virus's structural response, they identified key mechanisms driving its self-rolling behavior. Specifically, this model reveals how pressure differences, membrane curvature stiffness, and electrostatic interactions contribute to this phenomenon. Ultimately, this research sheds light on the underlying physics underlying virus-mediated membrane fusion.

This is the introductory paper to a series studying distorted galaxy shapes. Our initial focus is on "U-type" warps in galaxies. These warped galaxies exhibit a unique appearance, with their disks bent into a "U" shape, and are typically found in groups of many galaxies. Our research identifies the following characteristics of these warped galaxies: they have moderate levels of warping, limited colors, and are relatively small in size. Conversely, galaxies with "C-type" warps, which have a closed ring structure, are typically found in isolation, and exhibit more pronounced warping along with brighter optical properties. Furthermore, approximately 56% of galaxies with "U-type" warps are found in regions with high galaxy density, whereas this is the case for only 26% of galaxies with "C-type" warps. Our findings also reveal that galaxies with "U-type" warps are more likely to display dust lanes and HII regions, indicating enhanced star formation activity. Additionally, these warped galaxies are more frequently found near the edges of groups. Conversely, those with "C-type" warps show no significant differences in terms of density or star formation activity. It's worth noting that galaxies with "U-type" warps share multiple similarities with jellyfish galaxies, which are thought to be resulting from the interaction between group members.

This research builds upon the concept of Liouville type theorems for dimensionally sublinear Ricci defects with constant scalar curvature. Building upon the foundation laid by Jia and Wang's recent paper, we apply this result to demonstrate the proof of multiple related theorems.

The lattice structures of potassium ($KBr_3$), rubidium ($Rb_3$), and caesium ($CsBr_3$), all exhibiting cubic symmetry with edges of identical length, have been proposed. It's found that the ideal $A$Bi$_2$ compounds adopt this structure, which features threefold rotational symmetry. The dynamic behavior of phonons in this type of structure may give rise to chiral modes. By applying the principles of group theory and coordinate transformation, the characteristics of phonon dispersion curves are determined, and the existence of chiral rings in the Brillouin zone is identified, which contains time-dependent modes that can be observed experimentally. The caesium ($CsBr_3$) compound shows chiral vibrations at its acoustic edge phase, a feature that can be either doped into or deleted by substituting biismuth with another element. Conversely, potassium ($KBr_3$) and rubidium ($Rb_3$) show chiral rings in their phonon spectrum, which contains both rigid and flexible movements, and can be either doped into or deleted by substituting biismuth with another element. The caesium ($CsBr_3$), however, shows vibrational modes that can be observed experimentally when it is in its natural state.

A comprehensive calculation of nonadiabatic Born effective coefficients for metals has been developed using a rigorous approach based on linear response theory and symmetry principles. Our methodology measures the mass associated with each type of charge carrier, which allows us to derive a mean effective mass for the entire system. By applying this framework, we computed the Born effective coefficients for gold, silver, and copper, and confirmed that their values are close to those previously reported. Additionally, we demonstrated that our method yields a comprehensive definition of the Drude mass, which encompasses contributions from both electrons and ions. Our findings also revealed that the conventional Born effective coefficients and the Drude mass are somewhat intentially connected.

Researchers obtain unparalleled insights into the intricate dynamics of fluids in turbulent motion by harnessing the power of ultra-low noise conditions. Despite this, the underlying mechanisms driving the transition from hydodynamic turbulence to thermohydodynamic turbulence remain poorly understood. Previous research utilized sophisticated measurement techniques to analyze turbulence in the range of dissipation, yielding promising results. To build upon these findings, a study employs a cutting-edge measurement tool with exceptional sensitivity to study turbulence in an ultra-low noise environment. By doing so, researchers are able to uncover intricate details within the energy spectrum and associated vorticity distribution in this turbulent range. Notably, their measurements fail to confirm the widely accepted Kobayashi-Yamamoto theory, instead revealing agreement with the classical Kolmogorov-Obukhov spectrum. To explain this discrepancy, the study proposes a new theoretical framework, which suggests that thermal disturbance gives rise to a spiral structure in vortices.
