By examining a two-qubit system, we explore both entangled and contextually dependent states within this framework, revealing that all contextually dependent states become entangled when measured, whereas the reverse is not necessarily true, showcasing a distinct form of contextuality associated with the $E_8$ root system. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between contextuality and nonclassicality, where contextuality does not necessarily imply nonclassicality, and propose future research avenues to delve into the intricacies of quantum mechanics using the $E_8$ root system.

In the study of superconducting materials with exceptional electronic properties, 
it has been proposed that multi-body Cooper pairing can occur within one-dimensional
bands with flat energy profiles, despite the absence of Fermi surface physics. 
This unconventional pairing is made possible by interactions between extended wavefunction
components that reside on neighboring sites. 
In this research, a model incorporating strong spin-orbit coupling and
lattice effects is analyzed through a combination of analytical and numerical methods.
Results indicate that under certain conditions, the pairing tends toward
a $p$-wave symmetry with respect to momentum, while also being sensitive
to magnetic fields and showing signs of pair density wave phases. 
We hope that exploring this multi-body Cooper pairing will shed light on the inherent
properties of these superconducting materials and guide the investigation of
correlated phenomena in topological band superconductors.

Let $G$ be a connected, locally compact group that is not compact. In this note, we expand upon Polya's theorem, originally stated for $\mathbb{R}$, by providing conditions under which a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ is the Fourier transform of a tempered distribution on $\mathbb{R}$. Our proof is adapted from a similar argument in the case of discrete groups, as presented in Duffin-Schwarz's paper.

This research assesses the performance of eight clustering methods in a high-dimensional context where some of the variables are continuous and others are binary. The analysis utilizes a real-world dataset comprising existence-absence data on benthic species from 386 marine locations across Europe. The species' ecological roles are significantly impacted by environmental variables such as coastline protection levels, distances from sources of pollution, and ocean currents directions. The investigators evaluated the clustering methods using various criteria, including the stability of resulting clusters, effectiveness in identifying meaningful groups, and overall performance as assessed by the silhouette coefficient. The assessment of clustering results was facilitated through the incorporation of metrics like the Watson-Davis cluster stability index and novel modifications, allowing the comparison of stability between different numbers of clusters using graphical and statistical methods. The findings indicate that the silhouettes and Jaccard indices are reliable measures for assessing the quality of clustering partitions, while the Calinski-Harabasz index and the gap statistics are useful for determining the optimal number of clusters.

In computer vision, identifying salient items within an image is crucial for various applications, yet it poses significant challenges due to image complexity, object interdependence, and limited training data availability. Despite recent advances, accurately detecting salient items in images remains a difficult task, particularly when images contain multiple interacting objects or are of low quality. To address this, we propose an end-to-end deep learning network that integrates object disentanglement, depth-enhanced image fusion, and weighted image ranking to effectively identify salient items in RGB and RGB-D images. Our framework captures the primary features of images, separates objects into a background and foreground based on noise-reduced features, and enhances depth information to improve fusion and background suppression. Through extensive experiments on challenging datasets, our method demonstrates superior performance on background suppression, auxiliary information utilization, and generalization ability. Our framework's source code and models can be found at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/SEFI\_SIII.

This paper presents our system um-iu@ling, which recently participated in SemEval-2019's OffensEval Challenge. Our task was to identify and categorize offensive content across multiple platforms. Our multi-language, multi-task pipeline leveraged BERT models for feature extraction and Support Vector Machines for classification. Our final submissions comprised three datasets, each analyzed with a distinct set of BERT features. Our results from the BERT models were then combined with classification outcomes from SVMs trained on lexical, syntactic, and sentence-level n-gram features. Our approach successfully completed both tasks, particularly achieving a non-trivial combination of high macro F1 score and minimal feature count by utilizing BERT models. Um-iu@ling's system rankings placed 10th and 11th in task A and task B, respectively.

For a given natural number n, a palindromic figure is a number represented by n digits that reads the same forwards and backwards. Conversely, an antipalindromic figure is a number represented by n digits that does not read the same forwards and backwards. Let A(n) be the count of palindromic figures and B(n) be the count of antipalindromic figures, both for the range 0 to 10^(n-1). This note aims to derive expressions for A(n) and B(n) and examine their ratios as n approaches infinity.

Computed Tomography (CT) scans combine data from various X-ray energy levels, which necessitates a comprehensive reconstruction method for scanning multiple materials. The proposed framework addresses three pivotal challenges: restoring scanned data, mitigating noise, and analyzing material decomposition. It formulation is grounded in a non-convex variational problem, which involves a balance between accuracy and stability. The proposed algorithm achieves robust convergence in theory and is substantiated by numerical experiments, which include real-world data involving cow bones and artificial data simulating multiple materials.

This work focuses on developing a novel approach to generate handwritten text images for specific languages, typically classified as low-resource languages. Typically, synthetic text data is created using a predefined set of words or names based on the application, but this can result in text data that is too regular to accurately represent real-world handwriting. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a hand-crafted language model to control the generated text, ensuring it matches the desired attributes. To efficiently train the model, we developed a single-shot data creation method that generates multiple text examples simultaneously using a single forward pass. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming existing synthetic data methods on handwritten text recognition for languages that have only a limited amount of labeled training data available.

Using the Schnakenburg-Weinberger method, a new set of large-scale matrix elements was computed between the spins of protons and neutrons. These elements were then incorporated into a merged ab initio calculation involving the Argonne-Virginia Tech 18 potential, coupled with the Lagrange multipliers from the Senoglu-Gazak-Jansen '18 potential family, for the ground states of heavy nuclei ranging from $^{48}$Ca to $^{294}$Fl. By including the new matrix elements, substantial improvements were observed in the energy predictions, reducing the discrepancies with experimental values by approximately 30% on average, while also enhancing the overall overall energy resolution to 338 keV. Furthermore, the new calculation exhibited enhanced agreement with experimental data for numerous nuclei, including significant reductions in relative errors of up to four orders of magnitude.

Concepts of quantum topological phenomena are often unclear, leading to confusion in the literature. This study aims to establish a solid understanding of the essential ideas involved in topological quantum phases, specifically exploring the SSH model as a case study. It begins by defining various notions of quantum phase, phase, and bulk boundary correlation, as well as subspaces associated with eigenvalues. Next, it examines degenerate eigenvalues, symmetry, and zero modes in relation to topological properties. Finally, several examples are provided to demonstrate the interconnected nature of these concepts.

Let $\Omega$ be a convex open set in $\mathbb{C}$ or an analytic disc within $\mathbb{C}^n$. The space $H(\Omega)$ consists of all holomorphic functions on $\Omega$. For a positive measure $\mu$ in $\Omega$, the Gram space $H_{\mu}(\Omega)$ results from the inner product of $f\mapsto\int_{\Omega}f\,d\mu$ on $H(\Omega)$. A linear map between these spaces is said to be compactly controlled if and only if it has a compact counterpart when adjusted for scale. This paper proves that any linear map between Gram spaces for measures in convex sets or analytic discs is compactly controlled if and only if its adjoint has a compact counterpart. An alternative characterization of compactly controlled maps involves the basis consisting of monomials or analytic monomials.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method employed involves calculating a two-loop amplitude in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory and then using a projection operator to obtain the supergravity amplitude. The approach relies on an accurate calculation of the preamplitude, which includes accounting for boundary terms in the AdS Heun equations. The solution of the Dirichlet boundary problem yields a characterizing function enabling the identification of the amplitude via the Witten solution, ultimately facilitating the extension of the technique to higher-loop amplitudes.

This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator designed for GPU usage with a focus on reducing data movement. It replaces the traditional single memory pool approach, switching to a multiple pool method that categorizes memory allocations into predefined sizes to increase efficiency and lower memory waste. By utilizing concurrent techniques for managing memory pools, DyaSOAr minimizes conflicts during allocation and free operations, thus increasing speed. Our implementation demonstrates higher memory usage rates and significantly faster memory allocation and deallocation speeds compared to current best practices. Moreover, we have integrated DyaSOAr into the popular OpenCL framework and conducted extensive testing, revealing substantial performance improvements across various benchmarks. Our results show that using DyaSOAr can lead to a 1.5 to 2.5 times faster memory allocation and a 1.2 to 2.1 times faster memory deallocation.

We investigate the option of embedding the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry from $SO(10)$ grand unified theories into an $E6$ framework.  By examining three distinct $U(1)_X$ choices, we analyze the resulting quark-hadron phase transition and determine the desired properties for an additional dark matter candidate beyond the Higgs boson.  In particular, we identify the hard break-down scale for the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry, and assess its feasibility in terms of technical naturalness.  Furthermore, we evaluate the likelihood of observing the $Z_X$ and $X$ gauge bosons predicted by this framework at upcoming colliders such as the LHC, HL-LHC, ILC, CLIC, FCC-ee, and FCC-hh, as well as in beam dump experiments with the current LHCb or a proposed future exploration of new physics at the ALICE experiment, with its planned intensity upgrade, titled the Exploring Hyperon (EHyp).

Our research involves theoretical modeling of a long, thin tube subjected to internal pressure, examining how it reacts mechanically and predicting elastic deformation, buckling, and stretching under varying conditions of pressure and strain. The tube's material is modeled as an isotropic elastic substance. Our goal is to develop a comprehensive theoretical framework that can be applied to design and stabilize particle detectors, particularly those with a long, thin structure, by providing essential parameters for material selection, design, and stability analysis.

In various scenarios, such as medicine and self-driving technology, developers of probabilistic models known as Bayesian networks occasionally need to ensure their models won't be damaged by unexpected changes in reality. This required certainty, which we call "sturdiness assurances," can be very difficult to obtain (on the hardness of which we offer new evidence). To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative approximation method, leveraging the flexibility of probabilistic circuits, to ease the requirement that a Bayesian network's probabilities remain intact or shift slightly. We show this method allows for meaningful trade-offs between computational resource needs and the extent of potential adjustments in the model's parameters.

A model of interacting bosons is studied with repulsive bose-fermion interactions, where it's possible for the system to have a superfluid to supersolid phase transition. Using a Landau-Ginzburg theory, it's possible to stabilize this phase transition by introducing density waves. Analyzing the system's fluctuations, it's possible to calculate the phase boundaries between the superfluid to supersolid and normal states. Additionally, it's possible to calculate the thermal energy associated with these density waves in the supersolid phase.

A generalized quadrilateral is a graph consisting of four 3-reguli and eight 4-gons, with a two-to-one ratio of vertices to faces. In this work, we present a method for creating a partial Steiner arrangement of blocks in a generalized quadrilateral, based on a transitive neighbor code. This code assigns a block to each vertex, with the arrangement being transitive under the action of a dihedral group. Additionally, we demonstrate how to generate a neighbor-transitive code, allowing for the construction of a neighbor-transitive block design in a generalized quadrilateral, with the resulting Steiner arrangement being part of a partial linear space.

A novel method for determining the mass distribution within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in the Galaxy is presented. A 2D correlation analysis between the mass density map of the CMZ and the square of the radial velocity map enables researchers to derive both the mass and anisotropic velocity characteristics of the CMZ. A previous study utilizing this method found a mass density of approximately $10^{21}$ kg/m^2 and an anisotropic velocity factor of 2.3+/-0.1 for a specific CMZ region. When applying this method to different areas of the CMZ, varying radial velocities were found, suggesting that the mass arrangement changes depending on location. Additionally, we find that the determined mass densities align with those obtained using different techniques and that the anisotropic velocity factor matches the value obtained from another technique, offering further validation for the 2D correlation method.

Accurate measurement of dilute systems using a technique called X-ray Absorption Near edge Spectroscopy (XANES) can be challenging, due to limitations imposed by the low concentration of detectable species and those of the incident X-ray photons. Researchers typically resolve this issue by enhancing the sensitivity of detection and increasing the interaction between radiation and matter, via an intense and short-pulsed X-ray beam. However, this typically leads to non-linear interactions with negative consequences, such as increased scattering and background noise, which must be accounted for in the measurement process. A model proposing an increased number of electron groups near the absorbing atom, in addition to proper normalization of the XANES signal, is offered as a possible solution to this problem. This framework is then applied to a model dilute system, Fe-doped Si nanocrystals, to demonstrate its effectiveness. Results obtained from this framework indicate that a proper calculation of excitations within the dilute system is feasible with an intense X-ray beam, providing accurate linear and non-linear XANES observations.

This work presents a temperature sensor that operates over a broad range of voltages from 0.6V to 1.8V. The design utilizes the PTAT current source and a binary weighted GmR counter to achieve precise temperature measurement with minimal error. With minimal 1.06nJ energy consumption and 0.24{\deg}C accuracy, this design also offers {\pm}1.4{\deg}C error tolerance. The temperature sensor was fabricated using 0.5$\mu$m PMOS technology and has a 0.24{\deg}C error with 43{\mu}S switching time, as well as a 1.4{\deg}C error with 12{\mu}S switching time.

This research focuses on an entanglement preparation method that uses quantum scissors to create polarization entangled states. A single mode quantum field is both amplified and stimulated by spontaneous emission from a collection of three-level atoms, all operating in the same cavity. A pair of atoms is selected and the quantum field is "cut" at the point just before they prepare a distinct entangled state. Our study reveals that this process results in two entangled photons with a probability of $P_{\phi}=\frac{\Gamma_{a}^{2}\gamma^{2}}{(\Gamma_{a}+\Gamma_{b})^{2}\Gamma_{a}^{2}}$ occurring with the photon states of $|\phi_{+}\rangle$, $|\phi_{-}\rangle$, $|\phi_{\pm\pi/2}\rangle$, and $|\phi_{\pm\frac{2\pi}{3}}\rangle$ each having a 25% chance of occurrence. A similar approach can be applied to prepare other entangled states.

This paper explores the concept of euclidean spanners in the context of the internet. A particular type of network overlay is presented, which can approximate internet paths and maintain a sub-linear distance ratio to the optimal euclidean distance. This implies the network's hop distance is only logarithmically far from the optimal. This model relies on node pairs having consistent and known positions. This overlay can be achieved through distributed computation with a relatively small number of messages. The design also allows message content to be limited to small packet sizes, making it feasible for implementation. The authors also investigate how this overlay can be utilized in routing protocols to facilitate efficient network communication.

Accurate classification of IoT gadget data, comprised of diverse and time-stamped sensor readings, is crucial. However, common machine learning algorithms may fail to achieve satisfactory accuracy due to their susceptibility to inaccuracies in training data. Feature selection is a viable approach to improve model accuracy and robustness by eliminating redundant sensor measurements. Current methods rely on exhaustive calculations to compare features across different frames and are often impractical for complex IoT gadgets due to their multiple active sensor channels. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel, feature-agnostic framework that efficiently compares features within frames with a low computational expense. Our approach utilizes statistical analysis and is evaluated on IoT gadget datasets with multiple active sensor frames. We demonstrate that it outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency and achieves comparable accuracy using a diagonal variance normalization technique to compensate for noise in the datasets.

This study introduces a modal logic called KGL, which is an extension of Gödel modal logic. We generate mathematical structures for KGL to study its properties. We also explore variations of KGL as well as its relationships with other known modal logics.

This research presents a novel and efficient framework for translating unfamiliar technical terms during machine translation. Typically, statistical machine translation models are tailored to exploit in-domain training data to build extensive translation dictionaries. However, when confronted with unknown technical phrases in target languages, these models fall short due to a lack of direct parallel data. To address this challenge, our proposed framework harnesses bilingual external resources to generate accurate target phrases for unfamiliar source phrases. By incorporating a straightforward prediction model, it determines the most suitable target phrases based on extensive bilingual data. Moreover, to maintain computational efficiency, it enables term alignment to be performed on-the-fly during translation.

A distorted resolvent, an analytical tool, is introduced to establish global
Nash equilibria for a variety of Nash equilibrium concepts, including those
involving non-convex games, $L_p$-regret minimization, and quasi-concave/convex
games, utilizing parameters from the distorted resolvent.

I conducted an in-depth analysis of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) by simulating their gravitational influence on electromagnetic waves, employing the PopSyCLE code. This code enables the calculation of a PBH's profile based on its mass, spin, and gravitational potential. I subsequently developed a novel method to calculate the thermal profile of a PBH by linking the radiation and matter components using an equation of state.

Subsequently, I refined the PopSyCLE code to accurately determine the thermal profile of a PBH. Through simulations, I examined how a PBH's various properties affect its thermal behavior and, by extension, its impact on the radiation emitted during micro-lensing events. Furthermore, I discovered that an enhanced thermal flux is generated by a PBH with a significant spin component, as it produces a more pronounced gravitational effect, thereby intensifying the radiation emitted. Moreover, I identified a relationship between the PBH's infrared (IR) and millimeter wave emission, indicating that a more massive PBH is associated with longer emission wavelengths.

I also explored the potential to distinguish PBHs from continuous wave missions like OGLE through repeated PBH-related micro-lensing events. Specifically, I identified a more substantial deviation in the PBH-induced micro-lensing signal's amplitude around a certain mass range, which could potentially identify PBHs. Furthermore, I discovered that a more significant mass range of PBHs exists within which the micro-lensing signal's amplitude varies in a manner that differs

In a system where spherical bodies are packed in a two-dimensional space with a fixed density, the movement of a single wedge-forming agent is studied under the condition of having the minimum potential energy. The theory suggests the presence of two distinct phases, each exhibiting a different type of splay variation in the system. Moreover, the transition between these phases is found to be highly dependent on the system's density. Additionally, the possibility of encountering a complex phase with non-zero splay variation in the system is also considered.

This research expands upon stationary stochastic fields on the sphere, developing direct relationships between their spectral representations and spatial characteristics. We derive a series of one-step relationships between the field's spectral density and its spatial covariance, which are expressed in terms of the spherical harmonic coefficients of the field and the angular spectral density. Our work also addresses the practical challenges of numerically computing the spectral density from spatial covariance data and demonstrates how to apply our findings to both discrete and continuous spatial covariance functions.

A prominent benefit of quantum illumination over conventional sensing techniques emerges when considering scenarios with limited access to genuine photons. In such conditions, even single-pixel scanning methods can achieve superior results without necessitating double-pixel implementations or engagement with genuine photons during the measurement process. This can be accomplished with previously unexamined post-selection resources by implementing a single-pixel scheme that utilizes two-stage illumination, combining both bright and dark pulses in a quantum relationship. Additionally, this framework enables the creation of an effective negative correlation that aids in distinguishing genuine from artificial photons, thereby reaching a maximum value called the quantum benefit, which in an ideal scenario approaches 1 - 1/e for this specific single-pixel implementation.

The flow of a liquid through a foam with defects is heavily influenced by surface irregularities, resulting in significant resistance despite the pores' large size. Understanding the root cause of this resistance is crucial for optimizing fluid flow through materials with complex structures. Previous studies have focused on the effects of flow restrictions, such as pores with narrow openings, whereas this work investigates how surface obstructions due to foam defects impact fluid flow. By utilizing a mathematical model that accounts for surface roughness down to a sub-pore scale, researchers have dissected the impact of different types of obstructions, including those caused by T-pores, U-pores, and pores with surface wrinkles. Through numerical simulations, the law governing fluid flow resistance has been confirmed, and the associated constant has been measured for the first time. The research shows that this constant is directly proportional to the foam's viscosity and flow velocity, but is influenced by the surface tension when considering the effects of wetting factors. Furthermore, the study provides a mathematical representation of the foam's flow resistance constant and identifies its relationship with the Hertzian model, a framework commonly used in material science.

This research proposes an advanced deep learning approach that integrates data normalization with a comparative strategy for pinpointing irregular skin carcinoma samples. The goal is to enhance the accuracy of deep learning models in pinpointing irregular skin carcinoma samples through data enhancement and a comparative strategy that leverages pairwise image relationships. The proposed method excels in accurately locating irregular skin carcinoma samples with a relatively low error rate of 5.96%, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, experiments are conducted to analyze the proposed method's core components and demonstrate its practicality in real-world skin carcinoma diagnosis.

We employ ab initio molecular field approach to analyze the long-term behavior of electron holes in sodium. Our research reveals that the lifespan of heavy electron holes is directly proportional to the square of the absolute value of their momentum, a characteristic feature shared by those in lithium. In contrast, the behavior of lighter holes exhibits a dependence on the cube of the momentum. The underlying mechanism can be attributed to the interaction between the heavy hole and the next available state, ranked second, which is facilitated by the presence of state densities. The superposition of the heavy hole's wave function with not only the lowest but also the second-ranked state significantly influences this process.

Stochastic thermalization methods based on Liouville equation have proven effective, but they come with a drawback - changing the phase space volume, which invalidates the assumption of equal microstates and leads to incorrect results. Most proposed solutions to overcome this limitation are restricted to specific scenarios. This paper introduces an innovative method to solve this problem, retaining the essence of Hamiltonian-based approaches, to provide a general framework for correct calculations. We apply this method to the unbiased expansion of ideal gases in d dimensions, deriving thermodynamic properties in terms of available phase space volume. Interestingly, this approach yields the same general expressions as traditional methods, revealing a direct relationship between Hamiltonian dynamics and unconstrained phase space evolution.

This research extends the concept of graph curvature to a broader category known as oriented labeled graphs and introduces a corresponding invariant. It demonstrates that this curvature graph invariant possesses a specific property, namely that it calculates Kontsevich weights of local nature. To achieve this, we first created a suitable local coordinate system for symplectic sections, expressed the graph invariant in these coordinates, and established that its curvature meets the criteria for being a symplectic graph divisor, as defined by Berman et al. Finally, we proved that this curvature graph invariant is equivalent to the phase space graph curvature introduced by Stuart et al., which generalizes their previous work to multiple variables, and also to a symplectic graph divisor that represents the phase space graph curvature introduced by Berman et al.

Static imperfections within lightly nonlinear woodpile and binary granular chains can generate dynamic localized structures, whose formation is determined by the underlying potential curve's anatomy. When the potential curve is mildly asymmetric, a single equilibrium point forms, characterized by a periodic and traveling wave. As the asymmetry increases, the system undergoes a period doubling bifurcation, resulting in the emergence of coexisting periodic orbits. Conversely, when the asymmetry surpasses a critical threshold, a homogeneous state arises at the expense of these localized structures. Notably, we have identified a unique regime, dubbed the nanoptera regime, where multiple coherent structures coexist, and the implications of the nanoptera regime are far-reaching.

Exotic particles produced during the dawn of the universe, in the initial thermal and quantum states, can leave behind lasting imprints on the cosmic microwave background radiation, facilitating their initial feature detection. This detection can serve as a signal indicator, pointing to the existence of these particles. Our investigation into the initial feature paradox reveals a crucial connection between the magnitude of any distortion and the amount of energy produced, within the primordial quantum states, by pairs of particles, in relation to the initial thermal conditions. Moreover, in the scenario where the universe's temperature surpasses the particle mass, we find that emission from the quantum ground state dominates the pairs, while non-resonant pairs contribute more than resonant pairs, in the post-inflationary phase. Conversely, at higher energy epochs, resonant pairs become the dominant source. Moreover, our analysis indicates that, even if these particles are not detected through traditional methods, their signature can still be found in the primordial features of the cosmic radiation.

This study examines a square grid divided into alternating black and white squares, creating a gridline pattern. Two vertices of the grid are chosen at random, and a random "path" is generated through a series of line movements that allows the path to pass through the square grid, never touching the grid's boundaries. The path consists of horizontal and vertical line segments of length two, resulting in a Hamiltonian cycle. The research reveals that, despite the numerous possible square grids of size $n\times n$, with $n$ ranging from 3 to 25, the resulting Hamiltonian cycles formed by these paths exhibit significant structural commonality, including specific ring patterns and relationships within the squares. It was also found that the number of latticed matches in these squares correlates precisely with the number of Hamiltonian cycles, forming a quartic circulant graph. To establish this correlation, a precise algorithm was developed for converting the Hamiltonian cycles to latticed matches. The study presents a comprehensive mathematical link between two seemingly unrelated concepts, revealing a perfect correspondence between the two patterns.

We derive and validate a universal scaling theory for quantum dynamics in systems with a complex network structure. The proposed model, which builds upon Albert and Barabasi's paradigm of network growth, incorporates three distinct types of network components: early adopters that appear initially, rapidly rising trends, and long-standing traditions established early on. The dynamics of trends are characterized using Albert and Barabasi's scaling equations, taking into account the influence of recent developments and longstanding habits. The proposed model effectively captures the behavior of three-state quantum mechanics and generates predictions for the first and second moments of the distribution functions, which align closely with the observed data. Moreover, the model's framework is versatile and can be applied to other dynamical systems in a general sense.

Unlike traditional neural networks, optionally structured neural networks have the ability to develop internal features, or 'traits', within their non-linear components, without the influence of external rewards. The present paper examines self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer (ViT), revealing that it enables the emergence of traits, resulting in improved model performance. A thorough analysis of the characteristics of these traits is provided, including their relationship with symmetry and their resilience in the face of image transformations. Additionally, the researchers propose a method to purposefully nurture traits, using pseudo-self Supervision, which enhances ViT's performance on benchmark datasets. The code for this work can be found at https://github.com/flatmath/optionally_structured_vits.

In this research, we develop a combined dark model consisting of dark energy and a dissipative dark matter component. The model's dark matter part is governed by an equation of state similar to that of the Universe's fluidity, but with non-adiabatic behavior. The model's effectiveness is confirmed by using the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Markcian) method to analyze Hubble, Pantheon, Alcock-Paczyński, SnIa Hubble, and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations data. Our analysis reveals a specific value for the cosmological constant and a set of parameters that effectively describes the history of the Universe, including its expansion, from the early stages to the present day. We have also found that considering only Hubble data in the analysis leads to a solution with $\Omega_{de,0}=1$, causing the model to fail. However, incorporating other data types prevents this issue, enabling the model to accurately fit the Universe's history without restriction.
We demonstrate that the incompressible Euler equations are ill-posed in certain critical Sobolev spaces by providing a straightforward argument drawing on the properties of those spaces.

Recently, large language models have reached a milestone in natural language understanding, 
yet generating high-quality content consistently remains a significant challenge.
This paper presents a novel approach to this issue by leveraging the use of steady creative prompts.
To effectively capture the intended semantic meaning, a semantic similarity framework is introduced, 
which enables the calculation of a prompt's semantic distance from a set of reference texts.
The Creators, a type of neural art generator, is employed to produce diverse visual images corresponding to the prompts.
In the hidden latent realm of diffusion models, the creative prompts act as a bridge, 
connecting the visible image creation process to the underlying text meaning.
During training, the model adapts to recognize the steady creative prompts and associate them with meaningful visual outputs.
Ultimately, the diffusion model is able to produce high-quality images without requiring manual guidance.

A breakthrough in deep learning technique has revolutionized steganography by enhancing the steganalic redundancy threshold. Steganalic redundancy, which measures extra communication required over the original message, has been significantly minimized. Previous studies have demonstrated that anchoring probabilities in steganalysis using Bayesian neural networks yields superior results. By approximating the probability distribution of classification targets, this approach enables more accurate probability calculations. Nevertheless, current methods fail to utilize this probability density estimation for its full potential. This study introduces an innovative steganalysis method that leverages probability density estimation in a Bayesian framework. We develop a novel utility function that incorporates density estimation, ultimately yielding exceptional utility preservation and minimal steganalic redundancy. Moreover, our method ensures seamless compatibility with the current state-of-the-art techniques.

The main objective of this study is to explore the possibility of using the J/psi particle to detect light spinless mediators in neutrino and dark energy scenarios. The investigation centers around two types of processes: one involving the direct emission of the mediator followed by invisible particles appearing at the end, and another process where the mediator dominates the particle's decay. The analysis compares these predictions with the current experimental limitations on the J/psi decay into a pair of photons and invisible particles. The focus is particularly on searching for invisible particles at both the particle's rest frame and its laboratory frame. The study also incorporates the constraints imposed by the J/psi's mean lifetime and its decay into a muon and an electron, as well as considerations regarding the invisible particles' momentum at the muon electron decay frame. The analysis provides limits on the mediator mass and its coupling to the leptons, as well as the mass of the invisible particles. The implications of these findings on the efficient field theories of neutrino and dark energy are then analyzed. The limit on the mediator mass ranges from 1.4 GeV to 6.2 GeV, and the effect of these findings on the effective theories of neutrino and dark energy is then discussed. The analysis considers four different cases: the general low-mass limit, the QCD bound on neutrino, and two cases of dark energy with constraints on the universe's scale factor. The study finally concludes by highlighting the potential detection of the J/psi

Our analysis of solar data reveals that small magnetic disturbances observed on the sun's surface are associated with brief-duration high-speed movements of heated plasma. This conclusion is based on an in-depth examination of solar activity using the SDO/Focal Plane Project's high-cadence data. The finding that small-scale magnetic events are characterized by short-lived movements of plasma could have significant implications for understanding the longer-duration fluctuations in sunspot areas. The discovery also validates a theoretical model of solar activity in which active regions on the sun's surface produce distinct patterns of motion. The model suggests that larger-scale magnetic interactions on the sun are composed of smaller-duration (typically several minutes) simultaneous movements of adjacent plasma areas, which we have verified through our data analysis.

Human minimal films contain extensive data on how people move in response to changing situations. This data can be used to improve and validate computational models of human movement by comparing their predictions to actual movements. This study compares two main types of dynamic identification models, focusing on their ability to accurately represent the complex movements seen in minimal films. It demonstrates the challenges these models face when trying to incorporate all the observable information into their structure, leading to overly complex models that are difficult to work with. To resolve this issue, the researchers propose a novel method for simplifying the models while still accurately representing the underlying patterns in human movement. This method acknowledges that minimal films only provide partial insights into human behavior, focusing on the unresolved issues rather than the often overly general nature of the models.

Enlarging upon the Dark Matter concept, which assumes ordinary matter only constitutes a small portion of, the paper explores an unconventional idea where an entire percentage of, but not necessarily all of, it consists of magnetic monopoles rather than particles requiring invisible evidence. To make this proposal more feasible, the paper introduces the notion of "Milli-Monopoloids," which are extremely small magnetic entities, approximately one-trillionth the weight of regular magnetic charges. These miniature mono-poles could potentially be detected using very small, ultra-sensitive devices capable of measuring magnetic effects, which could be set up either on high-altitude airplanes or in balloons that float in the stratosphere where cosmic radiation is minimal. Furthermore, the paper suggests that these microscopic mono-poles could be responsible for galactic magnetic fields that have endured over billions of years.

Accurate climate forecasting is crucial for numerous applications such as policy-making, resource management, and public health. Despite the considerable progress made by climate modeling, predicting precise daily climate data from existing records remains a persistent challenge. To address this issue, researchers have found that applying geospatial focusing in climate models can significantly improve prediction accuracy. Motivated by this discovery, a new climate forecasting network has been developed, featuring the Cross-Focus module, which integrates the concepts of shifting windows and overlapping attention to combine information from neighboring locations in a step-wise manner. Through its distinctive architecture, the network effectively extracts and consolidates spatial and temporal climate features from a climate image, enabling improved climate prediction. The proposed model achieves notable success on various climate datasets, outperforming existing models in accuracy and AUC scores.

We suggest two low-energy scalar particles called shadow matters, which are associated with ghost Higgs fields in recent proposals for three Higgs doublet frameworks with $S_3$ symmetry. By incorporating a linear combination of Higgs fields that breaks $S_3$ symmetry, we create frameworks where the required unitary conditions can be met. Within these frameworks, we identify potential shadow matter candidates and discuss how they can be detected, for example, through decay patterns into a mix of ghost and visible fermions. One such candidate has a mass around 800 MeV and could decay into a mixture of $\tau$ leptons and ghost nucleons, while another has a mass around 800 MeV and could decay into a mixture of electron and ghost nucleons.

The PPT quadrilateral hypothesis, a widely accepted notion, suggests that convex quadrilaterals with vertices being PPT states or random quantum states, exhibit the property that all their faces lie within the EPB region. We examined this hypothesis by analyzing a specific configuration of such quadrilaterals, establishing that the PPT hypothesis holds for all values less than $\sqrt{\frac{7}{9}}$. Despite this progress, the PPT hypothesis remains unproven for values greater than this threshold, and it remains to be seen whether it holds for all values up to 1.

In neurons, the processes of substance transport along microtubules and the activities of molecular motors are crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis by ensuring the timely and efficient transportation of proteins and other molecules.  To investigate transport regulations and cellular responses to alterations in motor activity or blockages, we develop and apply a multilevel optimization model combining ordinary and partial differential equations. This model represents microtubules as continuous pathways with attached cargo items, modeled as discrete blocks, moving under the influence of motor proteins. To optimize transport efficiency, we introduce control variables associated with motor activity, located at specific intervals along the microtubule. A cost function is also introduced to account for cargo retention. Through sensitivity analysis and optimization using an iterative gradient descent method, we find that our model can effectively determine the most efficient transportation strategies under various conditions. Furthermore, our research shows that by controlling motor activity, cells can respond to blockages by changing transportation policies, minimizing delays and increasing transport efficiency.

The underlying network infrastructure of modern banking systems is complex, with multiple interconnected components, requiring a more in-depth analysis than traditional methods. This study introduces NeMo, an extensive dataset-based methodology for identifying hidden patterns in these networks. By leveraging dense subgraphs called network motifs, NeMo extracts meaningful features from banking transaction data, revealing the temporal and spatial dynamics of node interactions. A case study demonstrates NeMo's effectiveness in discovering latent processes within real-world banking datasets.

Researchers have identified X-ray and radio emissions from a dwarf star that is transitioning into a black hole through a process known as an inductively coupled differential relativistic collapse.  The radio emissions are in the fast-cooling phase and originate from the collision of two speeding particles after they break free from the collapsing star's magnetic field lines.  The X-ray emissions, on the other hand, are in the slow-cooling phase and result from the impact of these particles on the star's remaining matter.  By studying the properties of the emitted photons, researchers have determined that the cooling time is around ten days and that the energy released during this period is in the tens of teraelectronvolts.  The study further reveals that this phenomenon may be a common occurrence in the universe and that such events could be observed by future space-based missions with greater sensitivity.  The research is documented in the journal Nature Astronomy, with additional details available through arXiv.

Three-body $\tau$-decays can be analyzed to gain insights into new physics by studying hadronic currents and shape factors. Hadronic currents composed of light vector mesons serve as a basic reference point for understanding the decay process. Shape factors for mesons other than light vectors have been established in the flat space theory and are being calculated in the shape factor expansion in the $1/m_\tau$ approximation. To determine hadronic currents and shape factors, one must account for the internal structure of hadrons through quark loops. This paper presents calculations of hadronic currents and shape factors accounting for the internal structure of hadrons, utilizing mass corrections for vector and pseudoscalar mesons and applying the $1/m_\tau$ approximation for vector mesons. By breaking down hadronic currents into vector and pseudoscalar contributions, the form factors can be directly compared to data, and the remaining components can be used to investigate potential issues in the tau lepton decay.

A generalized parameter was established to generate families of Tversky metrics, where one specific instance produced the Jaccard distance and another produced a distance that mirrors the normalized information distance. The relationship between these metrics was analyzed by constructing a metric space with binary functions as its elements. The results also revealed that the collection of Tversky metrics is contiguous, meaning it progressively scales between the Jaccard distance and the normalized information distance. The study further explored the behavior of these metrics in terms of stability and its relationship to contiguity.

Existing deblurring methods are primarily designed to handle still backgrounds, 
which isn't realistic, as movements in the background are often indistinguishable 
from movements in the foreground. This is particularly evident in videos captured 
from a moving camera. Most low-level computer vision tasks also assume a static 
environment. This would require all objects in the scene to be frozen, which is 
unrealistic and impractical for background movements. This research proposes an 
approach to address blurred images, taking into account both image and scene 
movements, by analyzing the differences between moving objects and the background 
using convolutional neural networks. This is achieved by examining the variations in 
local spatial contexts. This method can automatically detect the degree of movement 
among objects and determine the amount of blur in the scene. Experiments have been 
conducting using real-world images, applying this method to both single images and 
video sequences. This method demonstrates superior performance compared to current 
state-of-the-art techniques.

Achieving advanced artificial intelligence with artificial systems requires significant resources to store and process data. In contrast, biological systems efficiently solve complex problems. Neurobiologically grounded theoretical models suggest spiking neural networks can solve challenges more effectively than computational models. This study explores a self-organizing biological-inspired learning algorithm implemented using chemical reaction networks that mimic a binary classifier's behavior. The chemical reaction network, comprising multiple molecular species, emulates a learning spiking neuron and can solve binary classification problems. Furthermore, the chemical reaction network has been demonstrated to learn and solve a more complex task, the XOR problem, although it requires additional molecular species. This study also investigates the feasibility of using DNA-based chemical reaction networks to program molecular structures. The DNA-based reaction network exhibits high reliability but is limited by its small capacity to store and process information. This research contributes to the emerging field of bio-hardware and could enable the development of biological systems solving complex tasks, or inspiring other solutions due to its close relation with chemical reaction networks.

In an extension of the classic thorn in a Gaussian space problem, we investigate whether within any countable ultrapower of a ordered collection, there exists a sequence exhibiting a specific property, specifically, the presence of a continuous image of Baire space within its internal relations.

As research relies heavily on datasets, systematically evaluating their characteristics becomes essential.  Understanding the data from the get-go can alleviate problems later on, while also facilitating replication and verification.  This paper proposes a basic framework for dataset profiling, highlighting the advantages of doing so.  Although existing solutions exist, they fall short due to several constraints.  These constraints include a lack of awareness about upcoming datasets, limited control over data processing, and the difficulty in pinpointing problematic steps during analysis.  This paper argues that unique and independent profiling can help mitigate these issues, as demonstrated through a comparative analysis between profiling a dataset uniquely versus traditionally.  This unique profiling method involves creating a one-time complete profile just for a particular research project, as opposed to the common practice of relying on existing profiles or developing them gradually.  This unique profiling method offers several benefits, such as enhanced research quality, increased transparency, and better accountability.  However, it also raises several challenges, such as the computational expenses and the balance between investing time and time spent on data analysis.  This study seeks to initiate discussion about dataset profiling, as well as its critical role in data-driven research, through a comprehensive examination of the advantages and limitations of this approach.

Hadwiger's conjecture claims that if a graph's vertex coloration requires at least $t$ colors, then it includes a complete graph of order $t$. We've demonstrated that if a graph's vertex coloration requires at least $t$ colors, then it includes either a complete graph of order $t$ itself or, alternatively, a complete graph of order $t-1$ embedded within it. This outcome aligns with the findings of Patel and Tasan, who previously found that if a graph's vertex coloration requires at least $t$ colors, then it includes a complete graph of order $t-1$ embedded within it. Our contribution represents an enhancement, as it now also considers the inclusion of complete graphs of order $t$ itself. Our method of proof employs the principles of molecular embeddings introduced by Patel and Tasan.

This research introduces an advanced adaptive generalized correntropy-driven algorithm for smoothly restoring graph signal sequences. The novel method effectively tackles challenges like signal node misalignment, noisy observations, and an unknown kernel size by seamlessly incorporating an aligned kernel, a robust regression framework, and a size-learning strategy, respectively. Furthermore, we develop a robust adaptive algorithm for generalized correntropy-based graph signal recovery, which efficiently addresses noisy observations and can learn an optimal kernel size through size adaptation. The proposed algorithms are mathematically analyzed, and extensive simulation experiments validate their superior restoration performance compared to existing methods.

One key objective behind building quantum interferometers lies in measuring tiny changes in the spin-dependent quantum states, enabling precise measurement of external magnetic fields. This application has previously led to accurate measurements of magnetic fields hundreds of times stronger than the detection precision. However, we have now devised a new approach to our entangled spinor interferometer that enables the measurement of even weaker magnetic fields, ultimately allowing for the direct observation of quantum fluctuations in vacuum. This advancement paves the way for the development of highly sensitive gravitational wave detectors.

The focus of this research is on precise estimates for the initial eigenvalue of the nonlinear Robin problem involving the $p$-Laplace operator, where we aim to refine existing estimates derived in diazyan and kardalov2022, yielding stronger and more accurate results. Specifically, we establish new estimates for the first eigenvalue in relation to the Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, utilizing a quantitative version of the maximum principle.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) effectively process graph-based data, but the theoretical underpinnings of their operation are complex. We clarify the working of GCNNs by drawing an analogy to Matched Filtering, a well-established framework (also known as Linear Shift-Invariant Systems), providing intuitive insights along the way. Matched Filtering successfully filters out irrelevant signals, while highlighting the desired ones. In our interpretation, GCNNs emerge as powerful diagnostic tools, capable of scrutinizing graphs at various levels of detail, from overall structure to local sections. Just as filtering parameters influence matched filtering outcomes, GCNN parameters (like filters and activation functions) determine their effectiveness in analysing graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate how disparate GCNN configurations might produce equivalent outcomes, much like different filtering systems might produce identical output signals. Notably, we showcase an instance where an ordinary Neural Network outperforms a GCNN in classification tasks, illustrating situations in which GCNNs might not be the best choice. Our interpretations also address common challenges like limited training data, hidden node connections, and inaccurate label assignments.

Transformers have brought unparalleled success to NLP, particularly with contextualized representations, which have significantly impacted parts of speech and dependency analysis by capturing context-specific word relationships. Contextualized dependency parsers have achieved impressive results, surpassing traditional models built on pre-trained word embeddings. Building upon this progress, many researchers have adapted contextualized models to supplement existing parsing models, creating self-learning strategies that combine the benefits of both approaches. However, these hybrid methods have only led to modest improvements. We have discovered that the main obstacle to further advancement is the difficulty in incorporating contextual relationships into the parsing models. Therefore, we have developed an advanced self-learning method that effectively integrates contextual relationships into parsing models, leading to substantial and consistent performance gains across a range of languages, including those with limited training resources.

A new analysis using the self-consistent light front quark model applies to the $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ transition process to determine shape factors for vector and axial-vector currents. By representing the $B\rightarrow D$ transition form factor and light front wave function of $D$ meson with respect to momentum and mass, respectively, the study can compare theory with experimental data and perform precision tests. Calculated shape factors for various $\ell$ are provided in the public domain. This work can enhance quark model description and predict accuracy for other transition form factors and decay properties.

We're investigating a quantum field theory where the gauge symmetry isn't preserved under time evolution, resulting in two distinct forms of BRST symmetry. By utilizing a brane construction, we present a method for identifying novel solutions to BRST cohomologies that translate to physical states with memory, describing charged particles moving through time. Our work draws from elements in ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, u(2) Chern-Simons theory, and the Wess-Zumino gauge.

Researchers extended polynomial-duration transducers, a previously restricted theory, to a more comprehensive framework without asymptotic equivalence to logarithmic space. This new theory, called unrestricted polynomial-duration, has a corresponding recognition algorithm with polynomial-time complexity. The proof relies on the existence of a specific construct, which is confirmed by constructing a novel, exponentially-sized graph within logarithmic space. The study integrates unrestricted polynomial-duration transducers into existing framework, resulting in a complete classification with eight distinct classes, guided by a composition ordering. The primary technical achievement involves demonstrating a key preservation property, showing that certain networks can be reduced to a specific form of flow-based networks, called CFIM networks, which in turn can be further reduced to a specific type of deterministic transducer, called mc-matters. The proof of this reduction involves intricate network analysis, involving multiple reductions, including one that relies on an unlikely hypothesis called the cone conjecture. The study concludes with several open problems, including a specific reduction hypothesis, called the mc-matters hypothesis.

In a comprehensive investigation, we explored how the basic chemical properties of Bi-doped Eu2Ir2O7 change as the degree of Bi doping increases. Our study revealed that Bi doping causes a significant increase in conductivity, but only a small increase in oxygen deficiency. Our analysis of core-level spectra showed minor alterations in energy position and ligand field splitting, but these effects are not sufficient to account for the substantial variations in transport behavior. Our investigation of near-core-level spectra, on the other hand, identified some significant changes, including the displacement of Bi 5d components and the growth of a gap-like feature at the Fermi level. These observations support the hypothesis that Bi2+ ions take on 5d octahedral sites in Eu2Ir2O7 and that the percolation of Bi 5d electrons, rather than Bi doping itself, triggers the insulator-to-conductor transition in Eu2Ir2O7.

Low-dimensional set-valued functions are fundamental in modeling processes involving minimal friction or resistance.  Two main categories exist: functions defined on a one-dimensional space with multi-dimensional targets, and functions defined on two-dimensional spaces with single-dimensional targets.  These functions facilitate the modeling of systems with low complexity, such as equilibrium states, evolutionary processes, and optimal control scenarios.  However, the low-dimensional framework presents challenges: it is difficult to find set-valued solutions that meet precise criteria, and it is hard to determine the properties of these functions, especially their continuity and differentiability.  Even when set-valued functions have these desirable properties, it can be difficult to determine if they have unique hearts - components with specific characteristics.  Two important criteria for a set-valued function, especially in modeling, are its Lipschitzianity and the presence of a unique heart with the lowest possible dimension.  This research contributes to our understanding of set-valued functions by developing models of their hearts under various conditions and testing these models to find their images.  It is the first mathematical theory to describe the structure of low-dimensional set-valued functions defined on a two-dimensional space with single-dimensional targets that take advantage of their potential fractal nature.  The study provides the most efficient methods available for constructing set-valued functions under certain conditions and proves the effectiveness of these constructions.  It is the first research to demonstrate that the presence of a unique heart with the lowest possible dimension can be both a necessary and sufficient

It has been demonstrated that the likelihood principle is not only violated by Simpson's paradox, but also by situations where data likelihoods form a complete circular sequence or multiple connected sequences. Simpson's paradox, characterized by a phenomenon where a dataset's global statistics contradict its component groups, is typically attributed to differences in baselines, but actually arises from the cumulative effect of overlapping likelihoods. Our work provides a framework for quantifying circular and nontransitive likelihoods and offers a new explanation for Simpson's paradox. Moreover, we have prepared an interactive online template enables researchers to create and visualize demonstrations of circular and nontransitive likelihoods.

Most machine learning models are developed using specialized tools, requiring compile-time configuration to set up, often leaving unused resources in memory at run-time. A recent technique allows compilers to replace compile-time setup code with optimized run-time code, eliminating unnecessary dependencies. Our study examines how this specialization affects the resource usage of common tools used in machine learning model training. We investigated five tools - OpenBLAS, OpenTBB, OpenCV, CuDNN, and MKL-FFTW - frequently employed in machine learning operations, and analyzed how their code setup could be specialized for resource optimization. Our findings show that compensating the initial memory allocation, the area of setup code can be significantly reduced, up to 94% in size, with some benefits also translating to performance improvements, up to 36% in case of MKL-FFTW, and noticeable speed enhancements, up to 11% in other cases, being highly dependent on specific program parameters, experiment setup, and hardware configuration.

Researchers propose a novel strategy for directly detecting sub-GeV dark matter, which involves looking for monopolar X-ray signals produced by dark matter scattering off nuclei at relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The intense monopolar radiation emitted by electrons in hot and dense astrophysical environments could mask the desired signal. However, due to the significant baryon-to-electron ratio in such settings, the proposed detection method can differentiate between the dark matter signal and cosmic electron backgrounds. The team also examines a second detection method that involves searching for previously unidentified, neutral X-ray radiation resulting from dark matter scattering. Ultimately, future nuclear experiments may be able to pinpoint sub-GeV dark matter using these indirect methods.

This paper proposes a method to achieve stable, symmetric transmission of quantum information for two discrete point dips in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. It's shown that contrasting entanglement dynamics between two distinct initial states results in either complete entanglement of the qubit and the cavity mode or maintenance of nonentangled qubits, respectively. Furthermore, the system's ability to transmit information reliably is linked to a combination of classical and quantum correlations between the cavity mode and the qubit. Two applications of this model are explored: one results in stable, symmetric point dips that support quantum information transmission, and the other yields stable, asymmetric dip structures without supporting information transmission. It's demonstrated that adjusting the qubit frequency enables control over the entanglement degree of the cavity mode, while maintaining nonentangled qubits. Finally, two discrete point dips in the system's emission spectra are identified, each with distinct entanglement properties.

Measuring inter-beat intervals provides insight into cardiovascular health, enabling the analysis of heart rate irregularity. Several machine learning techniques have been used to determine IBIs, yet they face challenges such as high error rates, complex model creation, and the requirement for extensive data processing. A new method is proposed to accurately calculate IBIs using the Tiramisu framework, offering a unique and efficient solution with reduced potential for errors.

This study examines deviations in an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle's behavior, which is influenced by multiple swimming robots, to better understand their collective movement. A modification is made to the particle's equation to account for the robots' nonlinear response, causing their movement to diverge from the particle's trajectory. To resolve these discrepancies, the researchers reworked the equation using variational techniques, which resulted in a new, simpler expression that aligns with the original particle dynamics when there are no swimming robots. To test the effectiveness of the new approach, the researchers conducted a series of simulations, which revealed that the corrected equation accurately describes the collective movement of the robots, particularly at lower swimming speeds. Additionally, the researchers discovered that the corrected equation can also be applied to a broader class of active particle models.

In everyday life, people interact with each other through diverse body language,
communicating complex information to achieve common goals. Current
approachesspecializing in the development of intelligent robots that follow programmatic instructions or
predict human behavior from visual representations, fall short in creating coherent interactions that
mirror real humans. This deficiency may be attributed to the lack of comprehensive data sets that capture
human movement from multiple perspectives or the unnecessary complexity added by prior approaches. To address
this gap, we present HUMBI, a vast collection of human body language, featuring 102 unique gestures performed
by 30 individuals, recorded through five distinct viewpoints and annotated with movement segment information.
Additionally, our platform includes interactive tools to help create, modify, and validate these data, aligning with
current standards in computer science. Building on HUMBI, we are hosting a contest to foster innovation and assess the
potential of existing methods to capture human body language. You can find more details about this contest, along
with other resources, at: https://humbi.github.io/contest/.

This research explores cross-lingual transfer in NLP at a detailed representation level, focusing on using task-specific maps to facilitate understanding and comparison across models and languages. We develop a new, flexible representation for NLP tasks that can be efficiently learned and saved, allowing us to leverage the expertise of fully-trained models in one language to inform processing in another. We show that these task depictions can be effectively used to enhance zero-shot translation, and that they provide a useful model-independent method for boosting low-resource language performance. Moreover, the technique is remarkably efficient, with nearly no additional computational requirements.

A key video super-resolution (VSR) technique, and fundamental to video processing, was introduced by BasicVSR, a model that employs explicit motion modeling and efficient template alignment for compact representation of temporal information. However, the original approach had limitations: it required a pre-defined motion field, which can be challenging for VSR templates to include various temporal dependencies, resulting in inadequate alignment of temporal factors in existing models. To address this, a refined model, BasicVSR++, is presented, featuring enhanced transmission and alignment, and is evaluated on Vid4 and RedVideo datasets with notable success.

This study investigates multi-task reinforcement learning using a symbolic system that can learn from structured task representations and generate modular policies, linking sub-tasks to predefined abstract task components. We observe that existing multi-task reinforcement learning methods often collapse when working on diverse task suites beyond their initial training context. In contrast, our proposed method, guided by a structured task ontology and reversible transformations, can learn to tackle various combinations of tasks, including ones it wasn't initially trained on. We evaluate our approach on both synthetic and game-like scenarios, demonstrating its enhanced generalizability and efficiency when compared to a method that doesn't use a task ontology and must learn policies for each task separately. While our results show that a method without a task ontology can perform as well as our approach in a task suite it was trained on, our approach significantly outperforms it in a larger, more diverse task suite and requires substantially fewer training trials.

Working in the spirit of Bennett's  Tony, we've explored the limitations of some theoretical heat engines. Unlike classic models, these engines have finite power outputs and operate within limited timeframes. Traditionally, these systems are enabled to fully exploit their maximum efficiency potential through unrestrictive control over key system parameters. In this research, we've imposed a more realistic scenario, assuming that these controlling parameters are modified infrequently, resulting in additional limitations on performance. Mathematically, we've employed the maximum entropy principle and applied the results to two common thermal machines, deriving new efficiency bounds for both the Minimally Controlled Heat Engine (MCHE) and the Minimally Controlling Heat Engine (MCHI). Interestingly, these new efficiency bounds resemble the results for a classic heat engine, with an essential difference being that the maximum efficiency potential is now measured in terms of 'instantaneous' values rather than 'optimally realized' values. Furthermore, we've validated these findings through a numerical analysis based on a realistic scenario involving a three-level system.

This research aims to identify how energy systems in different US states are impacted by hurricanes and strong storms. To achieve this, a dataset of significant storms in the US between 1960 and 2020 is constructed, along with related spatial and temporal profiles. Utilizing a weighted least squares model, the analytical method calculates the statistical influence of storm intensity and duration on energy system disruptions. Findings reveal that hurricanes specifically target energy infrastructure in the Gulf Coast, causing prolonged outages in states like Texas and Mississippi. In contrast, states like Maine and Oregon experience brief disruptions due to non-precipitation related storms, while states like North Carolina and New Jersey suffer the most severe disruptions from all types of storms. Moreover, regions with high electricity generation vulnerability to hurricanes are heavily reliant on gas-fired power plants, which are often affected by storm-related wind and freezing weather.

In this study, we prove an extension of the three spheres theorem for monogenic functions under Clifford analysis framework. Specifically, given a monogenic function defined within a bounded domain V in a R^n+1 space, we demonstrate that it can be expressed as a sum of three unique polynomials, each confined to a distinct sphere centered on the origin. These spheres lie within V and have radii determined by the function's growth rate in three-dimensional spaces. This finding validates the original three spheres theorem for harmonic functions and establishes analogous results for functions governed by the Dirac and Kahananukko operators under specific conditions.

This rigorous investigation into two types of heterochaos baker maps, $\beta$ and $\delta$, reveals that these systems exhibit a wide range of behavior, from order to complete chaos, facilitated by a new dynamic, termed the 'collapse of approachability,' where ergodicity and proximity to equilibrium are compromised. Research shows that the success of Lyapunov geometry and the collapse of approachability can be understood within the context of a modified Dyck system, where the correlation between binary sequences and ergodicity is clearly defined. The study also measures chaos by translating entropy differences into a quantifiable metric, demonstrating that the correlation between sequence and ergodicity is directly linked to this metric. Finally, the research presents a theoretical threshold, $\beta_{MO}$, that systems must surpass to become ergodically complex, yet fails to resolve the uncertainty surrounding the value of $\beta_{MO}$.

In this study, we explore the possibility of prolonging the lifespan of scalar particles in their decay paths. This involves examining scalar sectors with extended periods of stability, which may lead to the generation of leptoquarks, flavor-changing neutral scalars, and inert scalars. These stable periods could potentially be created during the breakdown of $Z_2$ discrete symmetries in models like the inert doublet model (IDM) and its extensions. The main focus of our research is to investigate the prolongation of scalar lifetimes in the IDM and its Higgs portal variations, as well as in models with scalar leptoquarks coupled to neutrinos via the Higgs field. This analysis is carried out by calculating the thermal width within the two-loop approximation, taking into account that the IDM and its Higgs portal models exhibit the prolongation of scalar stability through the enhancement of scalar mass, while scalar leptoquarks combined with neutrinos via the Higgs field experience prolongation of their stability due to interaction with the Higgs field. The study also estimates the impact of prolongation on the production and decay processes of these stable scalar particles at future high-energy colliders, considering the prolongation of scalar stability primarily at the $pp$ collider with a center-of-mass energy of 14 TeV. Ultimately, this study aims to facilitate the detection and verification of scalar stability at future high-energy colliders, specifically with the completion of the LHC and the upcoming realization of the

This paper presents a generative framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, an enhanced version of the WaveNet model, to produce raw audio time series. The new framework incorporates a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network to generate waveform patterns, facilitating autoregressive production. The framework includes a pre-net feature extraction component, an encoding scheme, and a permutation invariant way for scalar prediction, which enables quasi-periodic prediction. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application in generating raw audio, including speech, music, and instrumental sounds, as evidenced by its high quality outputs and the diversity of generated sequences.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant technique, have become an integral part of daily life, enhancing user experiences and contributing significantly to revenue growth across various industries. However, CF's reliance on robust user-item interaction data can lead to poor predictive accuracy due to system sparsity, inaccurate predictions due to rating subjectiveness, and performance degradation as interactions diminish over time. Alternatively, Biclustering approaches analyze both users and items simultaneously to develop and refine preference maps, addressing these issue more effectively. Existing biclustering methods, although showing promise, have not been thoroughly evaluated for their predictive capabilities. This research introduces an innovative Bicluster-based CF framework, incorporating Biclustering patterns in the prediction process. Furthermore, this work presents the Biclf framework, enhancing Biclustering's restrictive assumptions, and proposes an evaluation procedure to assess Biclustering's predictive power. Experimental results on real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of Biclustering, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing CF methods, with particular success in scenarios with limited data, small or extremely large item sets.

This research aims to understand how magnetic activity affects solar oscillation observations and identifies reliable indicators of solar activity that can be applied to exoplanet missions. We analyzed data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, looking at how solar magnetic activity influences solar cycles and identified promising indicators of solar activity. These indicators will be incorporated into a model to predict solar activity for Earth-like planets around low-mass stars.

A key indicator that Majorana modes are present at the end of a Majorana island connected to resistive electrodes is found in the tunneling spectroscopy conductance, which shows Ohmic, quadratic-in-temperature, dissipation due to interactions with resistive electrodes beyond non-perturbative limits. This occurs because Majorana modes have non-zero total spin, allowing them to interact with the resistive electrodes in a way that produces significant, heat-due-to-friction-induced dissipation beyond non-perturbative limits.
