This level of understanding can be applied to detect Majorana modes in various systems by measuring the resistance and temperature of tunneling spectroscopy conductance, which indicates Majorana modes beyond non-perturbative limits.

Marking a functor adds structure to it by establishing a universal path, and this concept extends to bicategories through the use of shadows, which can be seen as bicategorical marks. This paper delves into the properties of shadows, demonstrating that they behave similarly to classical marks and have equivalent applications, such as marking subcategories and functors. In addition, the paper connects shadows to virtual and exotic marks, offering a new perspective on these concepts from the bicategorical mark perspective.

We introduce an image processing framework that analyzes a collection of images to create a style profile, which is then used to map a low dynamic range image to a high dynamic range representation. Both the global forward and reverse mapping processes employ a style-informed approach, facilitated by a neural network, to preserve the original image's details and features. The forward mapping process utilizes a non-linear transformation to expand image values, while the reverse mapping process employs a contrast enhancement algorithm to boost image high-frequency components. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively achieves a balance between preserving image features and adjusting pixel values. Additionally, the framework's ability to extract a style profile enables applications such as image enhancement, customization, and style replication across multiple image categories. The framework's universal nature is showcased through its successful implementation on various image datasets, including Lafreniere, KONIQ-0006, and FISHEYES. The PyTorch implementation of our method is available online at the repository URL provided.

This technical report outlines the rules and regulations of the AQTC Contest held during the 2022 Computer Vision Pattern Recognition conferences, detailing the objectives, evaluation criteria, and methodology of the contest. 

The report begins by explaining the purpose of the contest. To ensure fair assessment, we provide an objective evaluation protocol. Next, we outline the contest's technical requirements, including data preprocessing, model architecture, training, and inference protocols. We also define the evaluation metrics. The report concludes by summarizing the contest's rules and specifying the deadline for submission.

A remarkable phenomenon in atmospheric turbulence, selective sweeping, greatly amplifies the growth rate of rolling-circle cloud formation in snowflake creation, far exceeding conventional growth rates by a substantial margin. This process is characterized by particles being enveloped and carried along by swirling air currents, which, despite being stochastic, exhibit a surprising level of organization that facilitates rapid particle accumulation through a series of deliberate "catches." Previous research, including our own, has indeed observed selective sweeping in atmospheric turbulence, yet its underlying mechanistic basis remained unclear. Through a detailed analysis of large-scale atmospheric turbulence data, we reveal that the air currents' coordinated behavior is rooted in the inherent linear structures of the flow at the scale of large enough to influence weather patterns, which, in turn, cause particles to be caught in a deliberate and coordinated manner. A novel model based on these findings effectively replicates the coordinated air currents, thereby confirming the phenomenon of selective sweeping and its pivotal role in the rapid formation of rolling-circle clouds.

This research introduces a novel approach to robot navigation that relies on dynamic rules and adapts to new information on the robot's environment. Unlike existing methods that require extensive preprocessing, this method processes data in real-time and learns from its surroundings without a predetermined structure. Instead of using a predefined knowledge base, relevant information is extracted from experiences and incorporated into a dynamic database through a self-initiated reasoning process. This process employs an advanced deduction technique that simultaneously searches for connections and verifies relevance, and can be broken down into distinct phases that are transparent to users. Experiments using simulated environments confirmed the efficacy of this method in identifying meaningful relationships between various navigation tasks. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that this formal technique can be effectively translated into a practical implementation.

This research addresses the practical challenges of 3D sparse time-projection chamber data analysis, specifically reducing large datasets generated by cosmic rays. The number of data points in these datasets is proportional to $\sigma^{-2}$, making them impossible to process manually and difficult to extract features with current machine learning methods. A two-part neural network is proposed that both reduces data density and captures relevant information for event classification. The Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder outperforms current sparse data handling techniques and legacy neural networks, achieving dense data reconstruction with 98% accuracy and extracting key features from 97% of data points. The resulting data is suitable for feature-based machine learning models, yielding up to a 128x data reduction. The efficacy of this method has been demonstrated using 0.3 pb$^{-1}$ cosmic ray data collected with the TP-TPC detector at the CERN H4 chamber.

In the Finzi model, galaxy clusters are formed through a self-interaction process, where dark matter particles exchange scalar bosons with each other. Using the mean-field approximation, our study analyzes the galactic cluster's scalar potential using the Lorentzian distribution, and finds that the distribution of the potential's amplitude at a fixed radius varies inversely with the square of that radius. Additionally, our results on the average potential and its derivatives match those of previous studies, and our findings on the phase transitions in galaxy clusters align with those of the original Finzi model. We also make connections between our research to the Higgs boson and dark matter particle properties.

A type of geometric hypergraph is one where the intersections of its components resemble geometric shapes. This encompasses a range of applications, from the study of interconnected components in images to the investigation of certain types of networks. This paper explores a particular class of geometric hypergraphs linked to a problem originating from Tardos and Shor's study of a game. We identify challenges in fully resolving the problem and propose a related issue concerning the maximum number of 3-element subsets with a specific property within a set of n integers. We refer to this as the k-GEQ3 problem. Our proposals for addressing this issue include a upper bound based on a general approach for such problems and improved but still limited estimates derived from examining the specific structure of the k-GEQ3 problem.

To investigate particle-income patterns, the densities of low-lying states in $^{61,62,63}$V nuclei were calculated using the South Florida quantum shell-model. These studies reveal that unpaired  $p$-orbit protons in the $^{51}$V parent nucleus contribute to the angular momentum transfer, resulting in the excitation of a $d_{3/2}$ proton relative to a $d_{3/2}$ neutron. As a result, angular momentum-aligned $^{6}$Li targets can yield either head-on or tail-on couplings with significant $\alpha$-particle production. Analysis suggests that the $\alpha$-production cross-section is optimized at an energy near the Coulomb barrier, with the cross-section influenced by the specific relative atomic mass of the $^{6}$Li and $^{51}$V nuclei. These findings demonstrate that Li-V systems can serve as relevant models for studying particle-income patterns and can provide insight into the $\alpha$-process in heavy elements.

Inspired by the behavior of the Pacific Lamprey, this paper explores the utility of a neural network with adaptive spiking elements in processing tabular data with multiple objectives. 

The Pacific Lamprey's distinctive mating behavior involves a complex journey from the ocean to a freshwater environment, facilitated by an intricate system consisting of multiple sensory inputs, a highly developed brain, and a proprietary locomotory system.

Our model, which is driven by a motivated system, demonstrates the ability to learn from sensory inputs and use this information to navigate through a grid-based environment, matching the geographic progression of the Pacific Lamprey's migration route. 

This model has the added benefit of being resilient to data corruption motivated by the Pacific Lamprey's reliance on accurate sensory input for its mating journey. 

Our analysis examines the impact of various parameters on the model's progression and evaluates its multi-objective capabilities in a testing environment.

Our proposed protocol customizes and optimizes colon cancer treatment by matching 
patient-specific characteristics with the most effective therapeutic strategies.
By incorporating techniques from machine learning and collagen-induced immune reaction modeling, 
our process identifies the most suitable treatments for individual patients.
It begins with simulating the progression of colon cancer using a random walk agent-based model, 
followed by the determination of patient-specific parameters from agent trajectory patterns. 
These parameters are then utilized in a modified Fokker-Planck model to generate distribution maps of cancer cells, tumors, and immune cells. 
Collagen-induced immune reaction is represented by an external force field. 
To identify the most effective treatments, our protocol performs an optimization analysis based on various network measures.

The increasing demand for wireless communication is outpacing the capacity of traditional transmission methods, with a significant gap created by unused spectrum between device-to-device (D2D) connections. A new approach, known as immersive D2D, aims to fill this gap by enabling direct device interactions and creating immersive immersive experiences. However, the key challenge lies in managing the growing number of D2D links and optimizing spectrum allocation, a complex problem driven by frequent changes in network conditions, such as user movement and wireless signal interference. A new concept, called scheduling via deep learning, is proposed, offering an efficient solution that can adapt to dynamic and data-driven network environments. It leverages a deep neural network trained on real-time network data, such as geographical maps and interference patterns, to predict optimal D2D link configurations and spectrum allocations. Unlike traditional methods, it requires no prior knowledge and can handle unexpected changes, making it suitable for complex D2D scenarios. A performance evaluation demonstrates its efficiency, showing better performance than current scheduling techniques and neural optimization methods, with results improving as the number of D2D links increases. The potential gain in system capacity also increases, reaching up to 300% in some cases.

This research demonstrates that the helicity is preserved over time along solutions to the compressible Euler equations, particularly focusing on non-barotropic, viscous compressible flows in a domain without external forces. To achieve this, we first establish an equation for the conserved helicity, then prove its non-degeneracy, and finally show that it remains invariant over time along solutions to the compressible Euler equations. This result is analogous to a prior finding by Peon and Majumdar for incompressible flow in a domain with specific boundary conditions.

For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we find that the reflection coefficient has an absolute value of more than one in specific situations, which happens when certain conditions are met regarding wind direction and depth. The background three-dimensional flow meets certain criteria, and as a result, so does the two-dimensional perturbation. The circumstances in which this occurs involve an infinite number of interactions between waves and the mean flow. The conditions required can be realized through various methods, including altering wind patterns and water depth. The resulting behavior of the reflection coefficient is dependent on the signs of certain key components. The presence of multiple modes in the perturbation affects how the reflection coefficient behaves for different modes. The occurrence of a large reflection coefficient is tied to the presence of perturbation modes that interact in a particular way with the mean flow. The characteristics of these modes determine whether a large reflection coefficient will be observed, and if so, what its value will be. The background mean flow's properties are crucial in determining which perturbation modes will be active and thus influence the reflection coefficient's behavior. The properties of the background mean flow also determine the properties of the perturbation modes, and thus play a key role in determining the reflection coefficient's significant behavior.

Research on merging binary black hole events has revealed that many of these
binary black holes possess minimal initial deviations from idealized
orbitally circular paths. A theoretical framework has been developed to
accurately measure the likelihood of non-circular paths among these binary
systems, utilizing a framework that accounts for the effects of gravity on
motion, or post-Newtonian theory. By analyzing how merging binary black holes
are observed along the line of sight, researchers have quantified the influence
of non-circular paths on estimates of gravitational wave strain sensitivity.
Based on the current estimate of binary black hole eccentricity, it's
determined that stray eccentricity has a limited impact on standard gravitational
wave strain sensitivity, but may noticeably affect the accuracy of mass
estimates for certain detectors, with potential implications for accuracy in
future detectors with increased sensitivity.

Achieving high luminosity and coherent X-ray levels is crucial for diverse applications and research areas, yet the existing X-ray free-electron laser (FEL) user facilities have limitations in terms of either coherence or brightness. We propose a breakthrough solution, the "Brightseed" concept, which combines a free-electron laser oscillator (FEL-Osc) and serves as a pump for a subsequent radiation undulator to produce an enhanced, highly luminous, and coherent X-ray flux. The Brightseed's capability was validated through detailed modeling and numerical simulations. The scheme offers considerable economic benefits as it can leverage and complement existing third-generation synchrotron radiation facilities, making it more accessible and affordable to set up. The expected performance of this setup includes a high coherent X-ray flux at 10 nm wavelength of around 5 x 10^10 photons per second, a low emittance of 1.5 \mu m rad, and a low energy spread of 2 x 10^-4. The development of this innovative system will significantly expand the range of research possibilities at synchrotron radiation facilities and will also provide significant advantages for basic research and applications at existing and future coherent X-ray facilities.

Our focus is on detecting incidents in time-evolving networks, where nodes and connections appear, disappear, or change over time. To tackle this challenge, we developed an incident identification technique combining strategies for incident creation, incident representation, and rule learning to effectively identify incidents. Through testing on synthetic networks, our method demonstrated strong performance, particularly when compared to basic approaches using undirected or static network projections. Furthermore, we applied and refined our approach using real-world road transportation and air transportation networks.

Research demonstrates that in an homogeneous medium, a shock wave collapses due to the combination of an explosion's central pressure decrease and the medium's density increase. Our investigation extends this understanding to a non-homogeneous medium, specifically one with varying density, to determine how changes in density affect shock collapse. Our analysis shows that in a non-homogeneous medium, the critical factor influencing shock collapse is the rate at which the rear pressure behind the shock wave decreases, rather than the index of the medium's density. This is because the acceleration of the shock wave's precursor and the formation of a sonic surface drive the rapid rear pressure decrease. Our mathematical equations, however, do reveal a unique behavior in certain density functions. For example, when the index of the density function is less than -1, the shock wave may exhibit oscillatory behavior. Conversely, in a non-homogeneous medium with a density index between -1 and -3, the shock wave will continue to move forward, effecting a unique type of self-modifying explosion.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. This paper showcases the possibilities of requirements engineers contributing to the development of more effective explanations by collaboratively working with AI developers. A practical approach for incorporating explainability requirements is demonstrated, using a practical example that highlights how requirements engineers can facilitate the creation of meaningful explanations by aligning AI-generated outputs with users' needs and expectations.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize follow-up and treatment strategies, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for necrosis, nuclear abnormalities, and other signs of cancer. Accurate training for this task requires extensive datasets with detailed annotations. In this research, we present UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset of 12,000 histopathological images, including 6,000 annotated macroscopic views and 6,000 microscopic images, along with high-resolution ADC images for comparison. The dataset supports two main tasks: adenoma classification and grading. For the former, there are four possible outcomes, and for the latter, from one to four, making it a multiclass problem. In addition to the dataset, we propose an automated method for detecting and quantifying key features of adenomas. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in classification and prediction. UniToPatho is accessible online at www.unitopatho.com.

In a situation where a source encoder attempts to eliminate transmission errors, there may still be unintended data leaks occurring outside of standard decoding errors. We investigate the theoretical bounds of these data leaks from a information-theory standpoint. Our analysis reveals that data leaks can be comprehended through a linear perspective and that the leaks' zero-miss rate counterpart offers insights into the encoded data's coverage. Furthermore, we demonstrate that data leaks can be represented by a graph, where the rate of leaks corresponds to the size of specific clique families within that graph. This graphical framework enables the computation of the leaks' rate and tolerance via coefficient matrices and polynomial functions respectively. We also establish connections between the leaks' critical rate, tolerance, and combinatorial problems like the integer programming and the partitions with equal sums. Lastly, we present a study on the general source encoding with data leaks, which may be applicable to a variety of real-world data encoding scenarios.

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images obtained from remote sensing platforms suffer from degraded image quality due to limitations in antenna size and post-processing techniques, which necessitates image enhancement through super-resolution. This research introduces MrSARP, a novel hierarchical deep generative model designed to improve the resolution of full-polarization SAR images. The key components of MrSARP include a target image generator, a noise encoder, and polarimetry encoder, which work in tandem to generate high-resolution images and encode noise and polarimetric parameters for their respective roles. By optimizing the model's objectives, including generation of high-resolution images and noise-polarimetry consistency, the system is trained and evaluated using established metrics on realistic SAR images generated using the SAR-Lab simulator. Our experiments demonstrate MrSARP's capability to produce super-resolved images alongside accurate noise and polarimetric parameters, outperforming existing state-of-the-art models in image quality and overall performance.

A variation of Variational Quantum Algorithm for Optimization, incorporating Bayesian enhancement to QAOA, is proposed. By combining this modification with Bayesian uncertainty quantification, a practical method is developed to assess optimization results and forecast future outcomes. The rewards of incorporating Bayesian principles are examined using simulated and experimental outcomes, and the code is made accessible through a public GitHub repository.

This research proposes a precise method for identifying areas where two or more ellipses intersect. The proposed algorithm calculates the intersection regions between multiple ellipses in a systematic way, without relying on case-specific techniques or approximations that may lead to partial results. The algorithm can efficiently compute the complete intersection region between two ellipses in a time complexity of O(k), where k represents the number of intersections. This method has been verified to produce correct results for all possible cases and can be applied dynamically to determine the intersection regions between moving ellipses. The algorithm provides a means to determine whether an ellipse intersects a circle, a segment, or a rectangle, allowing its utilization in more complex applications such as game development and computer graphics.

In the ongoing process of learning, the model is continuously trained in real-time, without being switched off, allowing it to learn from uncurated, high-volume data streams. This approach is particularly relevant to situations involving learning from multi-step scenarios or mastering dynamic tasks that evolve with time. A model in a state of q-training remains active at any moment, leveraging previously acquired knowledge to make the most of newly acquired experience. This results in an always-updating representation of the world, enabling more efficient exploration of non-stationary environments. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of q-training in a variety of real-world settings, such as navigating complex 3D environments and mastering time-sensitive game tasks. This method also facilitates seamless policy transfer between related tasks, eliminating the need for frequent and labor-intensive training sessions.

A comprehensive study of magnetism has been carried out in a Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. In the context of infinite clusters, where the model's phase transitions can be precisely analyzed, the research explores the role of higher-order hopping parameters on magnetic phenomena. The predicted phase transitions from the ground-state diagram show significant discrepancies between short- and long-range-range hopping regimes. The study also examines the's order-by-disorder' mechanism, revealing that longer-range hopping parameters influence the spin textures of magnetic orders. The research provides a theoretical groundwork for understanding magnetism in triangular lattice Hubbard models across various hopping parameters.

Accurate vertebrae localization is crucial in various spinal conditions such as degenerative diseases, trauma, and spinal surgery, but the manual process is labor-intensive and time-consuming. A fully automated method using computational models to identify vertebrae based on CT scans has been developed without the need for initial localization. This system works by transforming the CT scan into a vertebral column-centered coordinate system and then using a vertebral body model to detect and position the vertebrae based on visible disc spaces and spinous processes. A likelihood map of the vertebrae is created and the model is adjusted to match landmarks such as the sacrum, L1, and ribs, to optimize placement. A verification system also identifies and rejects incorrect solutions. In tests using 21 CT scans, the system successfully positioned all vertebrae, with an accuracy of 85% or higher, and corrected common errors associated with fully automated approaches.

A mathematical framework exists for analyzing systems governed by multiple electrical currents, which are represented by a set of linear constraints on a polytope. This framework can be applied to statistical mechanics, where certain electrical currents are associated with specific degrees of freedom in quantum systems. This results in a region of validity within the polytope that determines allowed asymptotic behavior. This work explores the relationship between specific degrees of freedom and their associated currents, which are represented by complex numbers, while maintaining gauge invariance to ensure consistency across various representations. This approach allows investigating the variability of currents among multiple degenerate quantum states, which are calculated based on the system's characteristics and the method of spectral decomposition. To this end, a mathematical representation of the degenerate quantum states' variability is developed, which incorporates concepts from convex geometry and polytopes, while maintaining ease of computational applicability. This first paper establishes the foundational relationships between the asymptotic distributions of current covariances, polytope geometry, and the representation of quantum degrees of freedom. A subsequent paper will utilize these results to investigate the degeneracy of quantum systems.

This study investigates how certain symplectic properties are preserved under specific kinds of transformations on symplectic manifolds, specifically those that preserve the symplectic structure. It examines how these properties relate to the relative quantum homology of these manifolds, particularly under the impact of generators introduced through the transformation, and derives consequences for their quantum cohomology. The research demonstrates the existence of distinct symplectic structures, all of which are equivalent to a given reference structure under the specified kinds of transformations, and showcases some of these structures as examples. Additionally, the paper discusses implications of these findings for the study of Lagrangian spheres within these symplectic manifolds, specifically in the context of the conjectured/suggested Equidistribution of Bishara-Deglise-Faroutounian-Mishachev-Sivek-Zaslow.

The interaction between acoustic waves from one piezoelectric material to another is investigated through their poling directions and physical properties. When the materials are aligned perpendicularly, and the distance between them is in the order of the acoustic wavelength, nearly total transmission is observed, primarily Caused by the enhanced polarization effects that arise at the material interface. Furthermore, the experimental findings are supported by three-dimensional simulations, which confirm that the transmission coefficient is largely determined by the materials' electromechanical properties and the relative orientation of their electric dipoles. Notably, nearly 100% of the acoustic energy is transferred to the receiving piezoelectric material, yielding a high figure of merit. The characteristics of this acoustic interface, such as its small thickness, and the materials' closely positioned placement, may facilitate integration of piezoelectric sensors and actuators.

The J-band anomaly refers to an unusual brightness increase exhibited by the exoplanet K2-22b during certain partial eclipses, attributed to massive grain-sized particles in its atmosphere. In 2019, it was observed that K2-22b displays analogous anomalies at thermally induced partial eclipses, implying the presence of massive dust formations. We carried out comprehensive observations of K2-22b's 2019 eclipses using the Large Binocular Telescope's Lyot telescope, yielding precise photometric readings at five distinct wavelengths. These observations were later analyzed using the MCMC method to obtain optimal fits. The data show that K2-22b displays anomalies consistent with expectations, featuring longer post-eclipse decay periods and increased brightness levels. Notably, the 2019 eclipses revealed signs of dust falling back during primary phases, as well as distinct temporal variations in the anomaly amplitude. We obtained dust mass estimates ranging from 100 to 200 Earth masses, accompanied by enhanced mass loss rates from the host star. These enhanced mass loss rates contradict previous estimates, based on 2018 eclipses, which had suggested a one-to-two order decrease in mass loss rates under partial versus primary eclipses conditions. The current research suggests that the host star's mass loss rate increases by at least ten times under partial eclipses. The data also indicate that the atmospheric dust upper layer may possess complex structures, possibly featuring microscopic dust formations separated from larger dust particles by the host star's wind.

We establish a condition, based on coherence of the Milnor algebra, that ensures the coherence of the Milnor fiber and provide an example to illustrate this. Furthermore, we derive a novel criterion that links the coherence of the Milnor algebra to the smoothness of the parametric space, which is applicable in several parametric cases. This results in a significant refinement of theorems on Milnor fiber coherence. To prove these results, we use the properties of flatness of a crucial locus in the singular locus of the parametric space.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analysis. It enables users to easily work with data using the popular Pandas API they're familiar with in Python. Daany is completely.NET core-compliant, making it highly versatile and easily integratable into various.NET-based applications, including Visual Studio, MATLAB, and Python via the pydaany package. Developed under the Apache 2.0 license, Daany is freely accessible from the GitHub repository <https://github.com/brauny72/Daany>.

My research explores how mathematics, once a secondary pursuit in the 16th century, eclipsed philosophy in the scientific community during the Renaissance. Through its mathematical underpinnings, the scientific revolution incrementally distanced itself from philosophical roots. This process was facilitated by Galileo's students, who established mathematics as the dominant language of physics. By doing so, they effectively marginalized philosophical approaches to science, paving the way for mathematics to reign supreme in physics for centuries to come.

New perspectives on Saha's ionization are offered, taking into account effects which have previously been overlooked. It has been commonly believed that during the Big Bang, electrons and photons reached thermal equilibrium, causing protons to combine with electrons to form neutrons, which then combined with other electrons to form atoms, through a process governed by the laws of detailed balance. However, this simplified view neglects the impact of instantaneous quantum fluctuations on matter and radiation. By applying principles from statistical physics, it is revealed that these fluctuations could have simultaneously created pairs of neutrons, atoms, and ions with significant magntitudes. Furthermore, it is proposed that these influences may have contributed to the non-uniformity of elements in the universe through a feedback loop, in which matter and radiation became linked at an elemental level. This new perspective is supported by recent research on non-Gaussian fluctuations in the universe.

This study uses the Magnetohydrodynamics with Dynamic Integrated Particle-in-Cell (MHD-DIPIC) model to create an integrated simulation framework that includes two components: a Magnetohydrodynamics solver and a Particle-in-Cell model. The MHD solver handles the complex movements of plasma macrodomains, while the Particle-in-Cell model simulates the movements of plasma microdomains utilizing a fully kinetic approach. The integrated framework enables simulation of varied plasma scales within a single simulation code, enabling research on how various plasma scales interact. We examined magnetic island merging utilizing the integrated framework and validated its results against existing research involving separate integration and integration techniques. The study on magnetic island merging reveals details on how microscopic processes unfold during specific moments in the island's movement, as well as how they affect the overall plasma dynamics, which cannot be detected through typical quasi-linear analysis. The investigation also discusses how various parameters influence the island's movement at different plasma scales.

This paper introduces Amanuensis, a novel train-of-thought system designed to learn and adapt through hands-on interaction with coding novices. Unlike conventional intelligent writing tools, Amanuensis operates as a collaborative partner, working together with a beginner to produce code. As they collaborate, Amanuensis fine-tunes its understanding of the student's skills and learns to tailor its support to provide targeted assistance. By exploring this adaptive process, we uncover key insights into how humans learn to code and develop a framework for designing effective learning environments.
